questions.rationale: Six of 20 is 0.3 of the circle; 0.3 × 360° = 108°.

questions.prompt: A pie chart shows that 3/8 of 64 tickets were sold online. How many tickets were sold online?
questions.rationale: Find three eighths of 64: 64 ÷ 8 × 3 = 24 tickets.

parent_activity.prompt: Survey 20 people about three clearly defined choices. Record counts, calculate each sector angle, and draw and label a pie chart using a protractor.
checklist: Category counts add to the stated total.
Each angle matches its count and all angles total 360°.
Sectors are drawn and labelled to match the calculated angles.

lessons.coverage_note: Questions check sector fractions, angle calculation, and actual quantities; drawing accurate sectors requires the activity.

lessons.explanation: A useful investigation asks a clear, answerable question. Decide who or what to measure, collect relevant data fairly, choose a display that fits the data, and report what it suggests plus a limitation that could affect the conclusion.

worked_example.prompt: Plan a fair way to investigate whether students in one class sleep longer on weekends than on school nights.
steps: Ask each student to record sleep hours for one school night and one weekend night.
Compare the two sets of hours in a table or dot plot; note that one class may not represent all students.
worked_example.answer: The paired records can address the question for that class, with limited generalizability.

questions.prompt: Which question can be answered by collecting numeric data from students?
choices: How many minutes do students read each school night this week?
questions.rationale: It specifies a measurable quantity and a time period, so data can answer it.

questions.prompt: You recorded the number of books read by 25 students last month. Which display best shows how many students had each count?
choices: A dot plot with one dot per student
A pie chart of unrelated favorite colors
A line graph connecting students by name
questions.rationale: A dot plot can show the frequency of each numerical count clearly.

questions.prompt: A survey about lunch choices asked only 8 students from one table. Which is the strongest limitation to report?
choices: The results may not represent the whole school because the group was small and selected from one table.
The survey proves every student has the same choice.
The results apply to all schools.
questions.rationale: A small, non-random group may not represent the wider school population.

parent_activity.prompt: Investigate a question about a measurable habit in a small group. Write the question and sampling plan, collect relevant data, choose and make a suitable display, then report a finding and one limitation.
checklist: Question, participants, and data collection method are clearly stated.
Display matches the collected data and is labelled.
Report answers the question and names a realistic limitation.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check question quality, display choice, and limitations; they do not conduct a full investigation or establish a reliable population conclusion.

lessons.explanation: A population is the whole group; a sample is part. Convenient samples can mislead. Random selection gives everyone an equal chance, but chance can still produce an unrepresentative sample.

worked_example.prompt: A school asks 40 of its 800 pupils about lunch. Identify the population and sample. Why use a sample?
steps: The population is all 800 pupils; the sample is the 40 pupils asked.
Collecting 40 answers takes less time than collecting 800 answers.
worked_example.answer: Population: all 800 pupils. Sample: the 40 asked. Using a sample saves time.

questions.prompt: A library wants its members' views on opening hours. It randomly selects 30 of its 600 members. Which identifies the population and sample?
choices: Population: 30 selected members; sample: all 600 members.
Population: all 600 members; sample: 30 selected members.
Population: library staff; sample: all 600 members.
Population: all town residents; sample: library staff.
questions.rationale: The population is everyone whose views are being studied. The sample is the smaller group selected.

questions.prompt: To estimate how often town adults exercise, a survey asks only adults leaving a gym. Which problem and improvement fit?
choices: Likely underestimates exercise; ask only gym staff.
No likely bias; ask more people at the same gym.
Likely overestimates exercise; accept online volunteers only.
Likely overestimates exercise; randomly select from a complete list of town adults.
questions.rationale: Gym visitors likely exercise more than other adults. Random selection from the whole population avoids targeting gym users.

questions.prompt: A school has equal numbers in five year groups. Ten names are drawn randomly without replacement from the full register; seven are Year 7. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: This can happen by chance; equal selection chances do not guarantee a representative sample.
The draw must be unfair because each year group must supply exactly two pupils.
Year 7 must contain most of the school's pupils.
Choosing the ten nearest pupils would guarantee a more representative sample.
questions.rationale: Random selection allows uneven outcomes. Equal chances do not force each sample to match the population's proportions.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions partially check population/sample identification, bias direction, better selection, and chance imbalance. They do not assess independently explaining sampling decisions or conducting a survey.

lessons.explanation: Stack categories in the same order. Subtract a segment's bottom edge from its top edge. The bar's top is the total. A 100% bar shows shares, so groups of different sizes can be compared.

worked_example.prompt: A bar starts at 0. Walk goes from 0 to 6, bus from 6 to 14, and car from 14 to 19. How many students take the bus?
steps: The bus segment runs from 6 up to 14.
Subtract: 14 - 6 = 8, so 8 students take the bus.

questions.prompt: A snack bar starts at 0. Crackers end at 5, fruit ends at 13, and yogurt ends at 18. How many students chose fruit?
questions.rationale: Fruit runs from 5 to 13, so 13 - 5 = 8.

questions.prompt: A travel bar starts at 0. Walk ends at 4, bus ends at 11, and car ends at 17. How many students does the whole bar show?
questions.rationale: The bar starts at 0, so the top edge 17 is the total.

questions.prompt: Room A has 10 students, 4 of whom walk. Room B has 40 students, 8 of whom walk. On a 100% scale, how many percentage points higher is Room A's walk share than Room B's?
questions.rationale: Room A is 40% and Room B is 20%, so A is 20 points higher.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw one vertical stacked bar for walk 6, bus 9, and car 5. Stack walk, then bus, then car. Add a title, axis label, key, source, and a scale that reaches the total.
checklist: The three segments are stacked walk, bus, then car and match lengths 6, 9, and 5.
The scale reaches at least 20 and the bar top is at 20.
A title, axis label, key, and source are written and match the data.

lessons.coverage_note: These items partly check reading a segment, a bar total, and one share comparison. Drawing a full stacked bar is checked by the parent task, not by the quiz.

lessons.explanation: Categorical data name groups: nominal groups have no natural order, while ordinal groups do. Check entries for blanks or impossible values before counting. Category totals show the distribution; the category with the largest total is the mode. A column graph can show how counts are spread.

worked_example.prompt: A survey records favourite fruit: apple, pear, apple, blank, pear, apple. What is the mode after removing the blank?
steps: Remove the missing response; count apple = 3 and pear = 2.
Compare the counts; apple occurs most often.
worked_example.answer: Apple is the mode, with 3 responses.

questions.prompt: Which variable is ordinal?
questions.rationale: Ratings have a meaningful order from low to high.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet column should contain ages from 0 to 18. One entry is 240. What should you do before calculating totals?
choices: Check the source and correct or remove the impossible entry
questions.rationale: Check an impossible value before it affects the results.

questions.prompt: Counts of book choices are mystery 7, history 4, science 9. What is the mode, and how many more chose it than history?
questions.rationale: Science has the largest count; 9 − 4 = 5 more than history.

parent_activity.prompt: Together, inspect a small survey spreadsheet, flag blank or impossible entries, then make a category count table and describe its mode.
checklist: Identifies a blank or impossible entry and explains how it was handled
Counts each category and identifies the largest count

lessons.coverage_note: This partial check practices validation, category type, totals, differences and mode; it does not assess spreadsheet operation or full graph construction.

lessons.explanation: Mean absolute deviation (MAD) is the average distance from the mean. Find the mean, find each value’s non-negative distance from it, then average those distances. State the result in the data’s units. A larger MAD means more spread; MAD is zero only when every value is equal.

worked_example.prompt: Find the MAD of 2, 4, 6 minutes.
steps: Mean = (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4; distances are 2, 0, 2.
MAD = (2 + 0 + 2) / 3 = 4/3 minutes.

questions.prompt: Find the MAD of 3, 5, 7 points.
questions.rationale: The mean is 5; distances 2, 0, and 2 average to 4/3 points.

questions.prompt: Two runners have the same mean time. Runner A’s MAD is 2 seconds; Runner B’s is 7 seconds. Which is more consistent?
choices: Runner A, because the smaller MAD means times are nearer the mean
Runner B, because a larger MAD means less spread
They are equally consistent because their means match
questions.rationale: The smaller MAD means less variation around the shared mean.

questions.prompt: Find the MAD of 1, 1, 1, 9.
questions.rationale: The mean is 3; distances 2, 2, 2, and 6 average to 3.

lessons.coverage_note: This short quiz checks MAD calculation and comparing spread; it does not assess larger datasets or digital computation.

lessons.explanation: Mean uses every value, median is the middle after sorting, mode is most frequent, and range is maximum minus minimum. An extreme value can pull the mean; the median may better describe a typical value. Compare observed data directly, including centre and spread.

worked_example.prompt: For scores 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, find the mean, median, mode, and range.
steps: Mean = 30/5 = 6; sorted middle value = 3; mode = 3.
Range = 18−2 = 16; the high score pulls the mean above the median.
worked_example.answer: Mean 6, median 3, mode 3, range 16; median represents the typical score better here.

questions.prompt: For 4, 6, 6, 8, 11, what is the median?
questions.rationale: The sorted list has 6 in its middle position.

questions.prompt: Class A scores: 6, 7, 7, 8, 9. Class B: 2, 7, 7, 8, 11. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: A has a higher median and a smaller range
Both medians are 7; A has a smaller range
Both medians are 8; B has a smaller range
B has a higher median and a smaller range
questions.rationale: Both middle values are 7; ranges are 3 for A and 9 for B.

questions.prompt: For 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 52, which average best describes a typical value, and what is the range?
questions.rationale: The outlier raises the mean; the median is 12 and 52−10 = 42.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks measures, outlier influence, and observed-set comparison; it does not cover inference about wider populations.

lessons.explanation: A box plot uses minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum. The box spans the quartiles; whiskers reach the minimum and maximum. IQR is upper quartile minus lower quartile. Box plots summarize but do not reveal individual values, sample size, mean, clusters, or gaps.

worked_example.prompt: A box plot summary is 2, 5, 8, 11, 17. Find its IQR and range.

questions.prompt: A summary is minimum 4, lower quartile 7, median 10, upper quartile 15, maximum 19. What is the IQR?
questions.rationale: IQR is upper quartile minus lower quartile: 15−7 = 8.

questions.prompt: A box plot has lower quartile 20 and upper quartile 32. What does the box’s length represent?
choices: The middle half of the data spans 12 units
questions.rationale: The box spans the middle half; its IQR is 32−20 = 12.

questions.prompt: Two groups have the same median. Group A’s IQR is 4; Group B’s is 10. Which statement is supported?
choices: A’s middle half is less spread out
questions.rationale: A smaller IQR means the middle half is less spread out.

parent_activity.prompt: On paper, draw a labelled number line and box plot for the summary 1, 3, 5, 8, 12.
checklist: Labels minimum, quartiles, median, and maximum at the stated values
Draws the box from 3 to 8 with a median line at 5
Extends whiskers to 1 and 12

lessons.coverage_note: Checks basic construction values, IQR, and comparison; it does not assess full hand-drawn accuracy or every limitation of box plots.

lessons.explanation: Compare groups using matching categories and scales. Keep ordered categories in the same low-to-high order. Percentages help compare groups of different sizes; range measures numerical spread. Compare modes and distribution shape, and distinguish counts from percentages.

worked_example.prompt: Reading ratings are never, sometimes, often, always. Class A counts are 2, 3, 4, 1; Class B counts are 1, 2, 3, 4. Which class has a higher share of often-or-always ratings?
steps: A has 5 of 10 pupils in those categories: 5/10 = 50%.
B has 7 of 10: 7/10 = 70%, which is higher.
worked_example.answer: Class B has the higher share: 70% versus 50%.

questions.prompt: Class A has 12 pupils, 6 choosing often. Class B has 20 pupils, 8 choosing often. What is the larger percentage choosing often?
Jump distances (cm): Team A’s minimum is 110 and maximum is 150. Team B’s minimum is 120 and maximum is 155. What is the larger range, in cm?
questions.rationale: A’s range is 150 − 110 = 40 cm; B’s is 155 − 120 = 35 cm.

questions.prompt: Ratings use the order never, sometimes, often, always. A shared graph puts always before never. What is the main problem?
choices: The order misrepresents the rating scale
The graph must use percentages, not counts
questions.rationale: The categories should follow the same meaningful low-to-high order for both groups.

parent_activity.prompt: Use two small class datasets to create a side-by-side percentage chart with matching category order. Discuss one similarity and one difference.
checklist: Uses the same ordered categories and scale for both groups
Calculates percentages using each group’s total

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check percentages, range and ordered-category interpretation. They do not assess digital graph creation, modes or full distribution-shape analysis.

lessons.explanation: Describe numerical data using centre, spread, and shape. Note where values cluster, gaps, peaks, skew, and unusual values. Link each feature to what was measured. Similar centres can hide different spreads; a display alone cannot explain why a pattern occurred or prove it applies to another group.

worked_example.prompt: Test scores are 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 90. Describe the centre, spread, and unusual value.
steps: Most scores cluster from 48 to 53; the median is (51+52)/2 = 51.5.
The score 90 is unusually high and stretches the upper end.
worked_example.answer: The centre is about 51.5; most scores cluster from 48–53, with an unusually high 90.

questions.prompt: Reaction times in seconds are 0.28, 0.30, 0.31, 0.32, 0.90. Which description fits?
choices: Most cluster near 0.3 seconds, with a high unusual value
Values are evenly spread with no unusual value
Most cluster near 0.9 seconds, with a low unusual value
questions.rationale: Four values are near 0.3; 0.90 is separated on the high side.

questions.prompt: Two classes both average 60%. Class A’s scores are 55, 58, 60, 62, 65; Class B’s are 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. What does the shared mean hide?
choices: B’s scores are much more spread out
A’s scores are much more spread out
questions.rationale: B spans 80 points while A spans 10; equal means do not imply equal spread.

questions.prompt: A student records four reaction times near 0.3 seconds and one at 4.2 seconds. What is the soundest conclusion from these data alone?
choices: The 4.2-second value must be a recording error
The value is unusual and should be checked; its cause is unknown
All students in other groups will show the same pattern
questions.rationale: The value is unusual, but the data alone cannot establish its cause or generalize.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks context-aware centre, spread, shape, and cautious interpretation; it does not cover formal tests or prove causes.

lessons.explanation: A dot plot places one dot per observation above its value. Use equal intervals, show unrecorded values as gaps, and label the quantity and units. A stack’s height counts observations; it is not the data value.

worked_example.prompt: For 1, 2, 2, 4 books, how many observations are there, and what is the most common value?
steps: There are four values, so the plot has four dots total.
Two dots stack above 2, more than above any other value.
worked_example.answer: 4 observations; the most common value is 2 books.

questions.prompt: A dot plot has 5 dots above 3 minutes. What does that stack mean?
questions.rationale: Each dot represents one observation at the value below it.

questions.prompt: Data are 0, 2, 3, 4 seconds. How many observations are there, and what integer value is missing between the minimum and maximum?
questions.rationale: There are four data values; 1 is the only missing integer between 0 and 4.

questions.prompt: Books read are 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5. What are the maximum and most common value?
questions.rationale: The largest value is 5; 3 appears three times.

parent_activity.prompt: Together, draw a dot plot for 0, 1, 1, 3, 4 minutes. Mark every integer from 0 to 4, including the empty value 2.
checklist: Labels the number line in equal intervals with minutes
Places exactly one dot per observation and leaves 2 empty
Reports the total number of observations

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check counts, gaps, maximum, and most common value; the activity checks basic construction, not every possible scale.

lessons.explanation: A histogram displays numerical data grouped into continuous intervals. Use a continuous scale and touching bars. State the boundary rule, such as 140 ≤ h < 150, so a boundary value belongs to exactly one class. Bar height gives frequency; grouped data do not reveal exact individual values.

worked_example.prompt: Heights use intervals 140 ≤ h < 150 and 150 ≤ h < 160 cm. Which interval contains a pupil exactly 150 cm tall?
steps: The first interval includes values below 150, not 150 itself.
The second begins at 150 and includes values below 160.

questions.prompt: A histogram uses 130 ≤ h < 140 and 140 ≤ h < 150 cm. Where does a height of exactly 140 cm belong?
questions.rationale: The lower boundary 140 is included in the second interval.

questions.prompt: A histogram shows frequencies 5, 8, and 3 for consecutive 10 cm intervals. How many observations are shown?
questions.rationale: Add the class frequencies: 5 + 8 + 3 = 16.

questions.prompt: A class has 4 pupils in 140 ≤ h < 150 cm and 7 in 150 ≤ h < 160 cm. How many are at least 150 cm but shorter than 160 cm?
questions.rationale: That exact interval has frequency 7.

parent_activity.prompt: Sketch a histogram for grouped heights: 130–<140 cm: 3 pupils, 140–<150: 5, 150–<160: 2. Label axes and use touching bars.
checklist: Labels height intervals and frequency
Uses touching bars on a continuous numerical scale
States that exactly 140 cm enters the 140–<150 interval

lessons.coverage_note: Practice checks interval boundaries and frequency totals; it does not assess full distribution description or explain all differences from categorical bar charts.

lessons.explanation: Choose a display that suits the data: tables organize counts, bar charts compare categories, pictograms use a stated key, pie charts show parts of a whole, and line charts show change across ordered values. For a pie chart, each category’s angle is its fraction of the total multiplied by 360°.

worked_example.prompt: A survey has 10 votes: 5 for apples, 3 for pears, and 2 for grapes. Find the pie-chart angle for apples.
steps: Apples are 5/10 of all votes.

questions.prompt: A category has 4 of 12 votes. What angle represents it in a pie chart?
A pictogram key says one symbol represents 4 books. What count do 3 symbols represent?
questions.rationale: Three symbols represent 3 × 4 books.

questions.prompt: Daily temperatures are recorded for Monday through Friday. Which display best shows how the values change over those days?
questions.rationale: A line chart shows change across an ordered sequence of days.

parent_activity.prompt: Collect counts for three snack choices, make a frequency table, then draw a bar chart with a title, category labels and a frequency scale.
checklist: Records each category count accurately
Labels the chart and uses a consistent frequency scale

lessons.coverage_note: Practice samples pie-chart angles, pictogram keys and display choice; it does not assess construction of every listed chart type or grouped continuous-data tables.

lessons.explanation: Order values; find the median. Split into halves, excluding an odd list’s median. Each half’s median is a quartile. IQR is upper minus lower quartile. Conventions differ.

worked_example.prompt: Find the median, quartiles and IQR of puzzle times 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 minutes.
steps: The middle values are 4 and 6, so the median is (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5 minutes.
The halves are 1, 3, 4 and 6, 8, 10. Their medians are 3 and 8; IQR = 8 − 3 = 5 minutes.
worked_example.answer: Median: 5 minutes. Quartiles: 3 and 8 minutes. The middle half spans about 3–8 minutes, a spread of 5 minutes.

questions.prompt: For 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21, which gives (median, lower quartile, upper quartile)? Exclude the median when splitting.
questions.rationale: The median is 9. Excluding it leaves two five-value halves with medians 6 and 14.

questions.prompt: Puzzle times are 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15 minutes. Split into two equal halves. What is the IQR, in minutes?
questions.rationale: The lower half’s median is 4; the upper half’s median is 10. Their difference is 6 minutes.

questions.prompt: Puzzle times are 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21 minutes. Replace 21 with 40. Which statement correctly describes the changes and identifies the better summary of middle-half spread?
questions.rationale: Range uses the extremes: 21−3 becomes 40−3. Quartiles stay 6 and 14, so IQR stays 8 and resists this extreme change.

lessons.coverage_note: These are partial checks of quartiles, IQR and sensitivity to an extreme value using one convention. They do not assess other conventions or a full written justification.

lessons.explanation: A statistical question anticipates varying answers across a group (the population) for a measured attribute. Even a single summary value represents many differing values, unlike a question with one fixed fact.

worked_example.prompt: Decide whether 'How long do pupils in our class take to travel to school?' is a statistical question, and name the population and attribute.
steps: Check if answers vary: different pupils take different numbers of minutes, so it is statistical.
Identify who is studied and what is measured: the population is pupils in the class, and the attribute is travel time.
worked_example.answer: Statistical question; population: pupils in the class; attribute: travel time to school.

questions.prompt: Which question is a statistical question, and why?
choices: How many hours do club members sleep each night, because sleep times vary from person to person
How many days are in March, because March has 31 days to count
How tall is the school flagpole, because it is measured in metres
How many chairs are in the hall right now, because a group of chairs is counted
questions.rationale: Sleep times vary across members of the club, whereas the other questions each have a single fixed answer.

questions.prompt: A report answers 'How heavy are backpacks carried by pupils at this school?' with 'The median mass is 4.2 kg.' What does 4.2 kg represent?
choices: Every pupil at the school carries a backpack that is exactly 4.2 kg
A summary standing for many varying backpack masses across the school population
The total mass of all backpacks at the school combined
A single fixed fact showing backpack masses do not vary
questions.rationale: For a statistical question, a single summary value like a median stands for many differing values across the population.

questions.prompt: Why is 'How many members are in our choir?' NOT a statistical question, and which rewrite makes it statistical?
choices: It asks about people instead of measurements; rewrite: 'What is the choir room number?'
It is too short; rewrite: 'How many members and leaders are in our choir today?'
It has one fixed count; rewrite: 'How many minutes did each choir member practise this week?'
It uses a whole number; rewrite: 'Did the choir rehearsal start at 4:00 pm?'
questions.rationale: Total group size has one fixed answer, whereas weekly practice minutes vary from member to member across the choir.

parent_activity.prompt: Ask the learner to write one non-statistical question about household items and rewrite it into a statistical question, naming the population, attribute, and expected range of variation.
checklist: Explains why the original question has only one fixed answer
Rewrites the question so collected values are expected to vary across a group
Correctly names the population, attribute, and realistic variation expected

lessons.coverage_note: This multiple-choice check covers distinguishing statistical questions, identifying population and attribute, and selecting rewrites, while open-ended question formulation is checked in the discussion activity.

lessons.explanation: Before summarising data, report the number of observations (sum of frequencies, not rows), the attribute and group, the measuring tool, precision, and units. Recording methods can cause clusters at round numbers.

worked_example.prompt: A table of seedling heights measured with a ruler to the nearest 0.5 cm has 4 height rows with frequencies 3, 7, 6, and 4. How many observations (n) were recorded?
steps: Add the frequencies across all rows rather than counting the 4 rows: 3 + 7 + 6 + 4 = 20.
State the context with units and method: heights of 20 seedlings measured with a ruler to the nearest 0.5 cm.

questions.prompt: The frequency table shows hand spans measured with a ruler to the nearest 0.5 cm. How many observations (n) are in this data set?
questions.rationale: Add all frequencies (4 + 9 + 6 + 5 + 2 = 26) instead of counting the 5 rows or picking the largest frequency 9.

questions.prompt: Which statement gives a complete measurement context before summarising a data set?
choices: Reaction times of 30 pupils, measured with a drop-ruler timer to the nearest 0.01 seconds
30 numbers ranging from 0.15 to 0.32 with a median of 0.21
Lengths measured carefully by pupils during a class experiment
A table with 6 rows showing scores collected on Friday
questions.rationale: It reports n (30 pupils), the attribute (reaction times), the instrument (drop-ruler timer), precision (nearest 0.01), and units (seconds).

questions.prompt: In 40 self-reported daily reading times (in minutes), 29 values are 15, 30, 45, or 60, and none are 28 or 31. What best explains this bunching?
choices: Readers can only finish pages in exact 15-minute blocks
A stopwatch malfunctioned while timing each reader
The total number of observations is 4 instead of 40
People rounded self-reported estimates to quarter-hours rather than timing to the nearest minute
questions.rationale: Self-reported times often pile up at round multiples of 15 minutes because people estimate rather than measure precisely.

parent_activity.prompt: Have the learner measure the lengths of 6 books with a ruler or tape and write a complete context statement before calculating any summary value.
checklist: Reports the exact number of books (n = 6) and what dimension was measured
Names the measuring tool and the rounding precision used (such as nearest 0.1 cm)
Includes the measurement units in every reported value

lessons.coverage_note: This quiz checks finding n from frequencies, recognising complete context statements, and explaining rounding clusters, whereas hands-on measurement and recording require the practical activity.

lessons.explanation: A data summary reports count, measured attribute and units, shape, outliers, and a justified centre-and-spread pair: mean with MAD for symmetric data, or median with IQR for skewed data.

worked_example.prompt: Bus trip times (in minutes) for 25 trips timed by stopwatch mostly lie between 12 and 18 minutes, but three delays over 45 minutes create a long right tail. Choose and justify summary measures.
steps: Note the distribution shape: the right tail of extreme delays pulls the mean and MAD upward.
Select the median paired with the IQR (in minutes) because both resist skewed tails and outliers.
worked_example.answer: Use median and IQR (in minutes) because the trip times are right-skewed with high outliers.

questions.prompt: Lengths of 28 leaves measured with a ruler to the nearest mm form a roughly symmetric distribution from 42 mm to 58 mm with no outliers. Which paired summary and justification fit best?
choices: Mean and IQR in mm, because IQR always pairs with the mean
Mean and MAD in mm, because the distribution is roughly symmetric with no extreme values
Median and MAD in mm, because symmetric data require mixing measures
Mean only without units, because symmetric data have no variability
questions.rationale: Roughly symmetric distributions without outliers are summarised using the matched pair mean and MAD, reported with units (mm).

questions.prompt: For 30 pupils' walk times timed by watch to the nearest minute (Q1 = 9 min, median = 14 min, Q3 = 22 min, right-skewed with one 48-minute outlier), which rewrite of 'the average is 14' is complete?
choices: The average is 14 minutes and the range is 30 pupils
For 30 pupils, the mean is 14 and the IQR is 13

For 30 pupils' timed walks, the right-skewed times have median 14 minutes and IQR 13 minutes (middle half 9 to 22 minutes), with one 48-minute outlier. Median and IQR are appropriate because the right tail and extreme time make resistant measures preferable.
Most pupils take exactly 14 minutes to walk to school
questions.rationale: It states n (30), attribute, method, units (minutes), shape, the 48-minute outlier, and median with IQR justified as resistant to the right tail and outlier.

questions.prompt: A right-skewed set of 20 parcel masses (digital scale, nearest 0.1 kg) has Q1 = 2.1 kg, median = 2.6 kg, Q3 = 3.4 kg, and one 11.2 kg outlier. What is the IQR (in kg) that pairs with the median?
questions.rationale: For skewed data with an outlier, pair the median with the IQR: Q3 - Q1 = 3.4 - 2.1 = 1.3 kg.

parent_activity.prompt: Provide 7 measured durations with one extreme value (10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 35 minutes, timed by stopwatch) and ask the learner to write a complete data summary paragraph.
checklist: States n = 7, the attribute, how it was measured, and units (minutes)
Chooses median (12 minutes) and IQR (3 minutes) and justifies the choice by the 35-minute outlier
Describes both the main cluster (10 to 14 minutes) and the 35-minute deviation in context

lessons.coverage_note: These items check selecting matched centre-and-spread measures, calculating IQR, and identifying complete summaries; writing an original multi-part summary requires the parent activity.

lessons.explanation: Check that both samples are random and representative of their populations, weigh the centre difference against sample spread and sampling variation, and state qualified conclusions using 'probably' or 'on average'.

worked_example.prompt: Representative random samples of 20 words are drawn from Science Book A (mean 6.2 letters, MAD 0.9) and Science Book B (mean 4.4 letters, MAD 0.9). What inference is supported?
steps: Verify random sampling and compare the mean difference (6.2 - 4.4 = 1.8 letters) to the MAD (0.9 letters); the gap is 2 MADs.
State a qualified conclusion: words in Book A are probably longer on average, though not every word is longer.
worked_example.answer: Science Book A probably uses longer words on average than Science Book B.

questions.prompt: Two representative samples of 25 apples are randomly drawn from the populations of Orchard X (mean mass 165 g, MAD 8 g) and Orchard Y (mean mass 141 g, MAD 8 g). Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Apples in Orchard X are probably heavier on average than apples in Orchard Y
Every single apple in Orchard X is heavier than every apple in Orchard Y
The two orchards have identical average apple masses
No inference is possible without weighing every apple in both orchards
questions.rationale: Because both samples were randomly drawn from their orchard populations and the 24 g mean gap is 3 MADs, Orchard X apples are probably heavier on average.

questions.prompt: To compare fitness at two schools, someone times 15 volunteers from School P's running club and 15 randomly chosen pupils from School Q. Why is a school-wide conclusion invalid?
choices: Fifteen pupils is an odd sample size
School P's sample consists of running-club volunteers, so it is not a representative random sample of all School P pupils
Running times cannot be compared using sample means
Random selection was used at School Q instead of volunteers
questions.rationale: Running-club volunteers are likely fitter than typical pupils, biasing School P's sample so it cannot represent the whole school.

questions.prompt: Two random samples of 20 puzzle scores from Group M and Group N have sample medians of 52 and 51 points. Repeated random samples of size 20 from Group M alone have medians varying by about 4 points. What should you conclude?
choices: Group M definitely has a higher population median than Group N
Every member of Group M scored 1 point higher than Group N
The samples must be discarded because random sample medians never vary
The 1-point gap is smaller than the typical 4-point sampling variation, so it may be due to chance alone
questions.rationale: A 1-point difference between sample medians is not convincing when random samples from a single population routinely vary by about 4 points.

parent_activity.prompt: Discuss a headline claiming 'Survey of gym members proves Town A residents exercise more than Town B residents' and ask the learner to evaluate and rewrite it.
checklist: Explains why gym volunteers do not form a random, representative sample of a whole town
Identifies that small sample differences can arise by random chance
States a properly qualified comparative claim using words such as 'on average' or 'probably'

lessons.coverage_note: This quiz partially checks evaluating sample randomness, weighing centre differences against sampling variation, and choosing qualified claims, while open critique is practised in the discussion activity.

lessons.explanation: Use a random, reasonably representative sample to estimate a population proportion, count, or mean. Estimates are approximate. Biased samples may describe respondents without representing the whole population.

worked_example.prompt: Of 60 randomly sampled pupils, 18 walk to school. Assuming they reasonably represent the school's 900 pupils, estimate how many pupils walk.
steps: Find the sample proportion: 18 ÷ 60 = 0.3.
Estimate the school count: 0.3 × 900 = 270.
worked_example.answer: About 270 pupils walk to school; this is an estimate, not an exact count.

questions.prompt: In a reasonably representative random sample, 12 of 40 pupils bring lunch. The school has 400 pupils. Approximately how many bring lunch?
questions.rationale: The sample proportion is 12/40. Multiplying by 400 estimates about 120 pupils, not an exact count.

questions.prompt: Four randomly sampled pupils read for 20, 30, 40, and 50 minutes weekly. Assuming this sample reasonably represents the school, what is the estimated school mean, in minutes?
questions.rationale: The sample mean is 140 ÷ 4 = 35 minutes. A representative sample suggests a nearby population mean, but probably not exactly 35.

questions.prompt: An optional cycling-club survey gets 50 replies; 30 respondents cycle to school. The school has 1,000 pupils. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: Exactly 600 pupils in the school cycle.
The school's cycling percentage must be below 60%.
Randomly choosing among these replies would remove the sampling bias.
60% of respondents cycle; this sample cannot reliably estimate the whole school's percentage.
questions.rationale: Voluntary cycling-club replies are not a random school-wide sample. The respondents' percentage is known, but the school's percentage remains uncertain.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions partially check count estimation, mean estimation, and sampling assumptions. They do not assess collecting representative samples or measuring uncertainty.

lessons.explanation: Check overlap directly on a shared scale. With similar spreads, divide the mean gap by MAD or median gap by IQR. Larger ratios mean greater separation, not guaranteed overlap.

worked_example.prompt: Two teams have mean heights of 150 cm and 160 cm. Each team's MAD is 5 cm. How many MADs separate their means?
steps: Find the mean gap: 160 − 150 = 10 cm.
Divide by either team's MAD: 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
worked_example.answer: The means are 2 MADs apart. Check the actual height displays separately for overlap.

questions.prompt: Each entry is one height in cm. What interval do the teams' height ranges share?
questions.rationale: Both teams have heights at 150, 155 and 160 cm: three of each team's five heights lie in the shared interval.

questions.prompt: Two groups have mean scores of 12 and 18 points. Each has MAD 2 points. How many MADs separate their means?
questions.rationale: The mean gap is 6 points. Dividing by the shared MAD of 2 gives 3 MADs.

questions.prompt: A has values 0, 0, 0, 4; B has 1, 5, 5, 5. Their means are 1 and 4; both MADs are 1.5. Which statement correctly uses the ratio and checks overlap?
choices: Means are 2 MADs apart; one value from each group lies within the other group's range.
Means are 2 MADs apart; their ranges cannot overlap.
Means are 3 MADs apart; every value lies within the other group's range.
Means are 0.5 MADs apart; their ranges cannot overlap.
questions.rationale: The ratio is 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2. A's 4 lies within B's range; B's 1 lies within A's range.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw dot plots on one shared scale for two pairs: A: 0, 0, 2, 2 and B: 2, 2, 4, 4; C: 0, 0, 0, 4 and D: 1, 5, 5, 5. Both pairs have a 2-MAD mean gap. Compare their overlap, counting endpoints as inside a range. Finally, compare a 10-point mean gap when both groups have MAD 5 versus when both have MAD 2.
checklist: Plots every value on the shared scale, stacking repeats.
Identifies that half of each A/B group, but only one-quarter of each C/D group, lies within the other group's range despite equal 2-MAD gaps.
Calculates 2 MADs versus 5 MADs for the 10-point gap and explains that smaller spread makes the same gap relatively larger.

lessons.coverage_note: These quizzes partially check range overlap, mean-gap/MAD calculation and tail effects. Drawing and discussion need observation. Median-gap/IQR calculations and judging whether spreads are similar need further practice.

lessons.explanation: Random samples of the same size can give different estimates because they include different individuals by chance. The spread of sample estimates shows uncertainty; it is not the same as how spread out individual values are. A biased method can repeatedly miss the population value.

worked_example.prompt: Five random samples each contain 20 people. Their mean sleep times are 8.6, 8.8, 9.0, 9.1, and 9.3 hours. What do the means show?
steps: The sample means range from 8.6 to 9.3 hours, a spread of 0.7 hours.
Different selections can explain the differences; individual sleep times within a sample may vary much more.
worked_example.answer: The estimate varies by chance, so one sample mean is uncertain.

questions.prompt: A bag has red and blue counters. Three random samples of 10 counters have red proportions 0.3, 0.5, and 0.4. Why do the estimates differ?
choices: The proportions measure individual counter weight
questions.rationale: Random selections can differ even when the population stays the same.

questions.prompt: Five random samples of 20 have estimated proportions from 25% to 40%. What does this range tell you?
choices: A single estimate has some uncertainty
The sampling method is necessarily biased
questions.rationale: The spread shows how much estimates varied across these samples.

questions.prompt: A school surveys students in the library at lunchtime about library use. What is the main concern?
choices: The method may be biased toward library users
Random samples always have no variation
A larger sample must be less representative
questions.rationale: Library visitors are more likely to be included, creating consistent bias.

parent_activity.prompt: Five equally sized random samples from the same population give estimated red-item shares of 25%, 30%, 35%, 30%, and 40%. Ask the learner to compare these sample estimates, explain why they differ, and contrast this with repeatedly sampling only from a red-heavy corner of the population.
checklist: Attributes differing random-sample estimates to chance, without treating any different estimate as automatically wrong.
Identifies the estimates’ range from 25% to 40% (15 percentage points), and explains why one estimate cannot make a prediction certain.
Distinguishes variation between sample proportions from red/blue differences among individual items, and explains why a biased sampling method can create consistent error.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks sample variation, uncertainty, and bias; it does not simulate repeated sampling or calculate formal uncertainty measures. A parent-observed explanation checks sampling reasoning with supplied sample results; it does not require physical data collection.

lessons.explanation: A scatter graph shows paired values. Label each axis with its variable and units, then use equal steps on each scale. An upward pattern is positive correlation; a downward pattern is negative. A best-fit line follows the overall pattern, with points roughly balanced above and below; use it for estimates within the data range.

worked_example.prompt: A best-fit line for hours studied x and test score y is y = 10x + 40. Estimate the score at 3 hours.
steps: Substitute x = 3: y = 10 × 3 + 40.
Calculate 30 + 40 = 70.

questions.prompt: For a scatter graph of plant height in cm against days, which axis labels are suitable?
questions.rationale: Each axis should identify its variable, including the height unit.

questions.prompt: As outdoor temperature rises, ice-cream sales usually rise too. What correlation does this describe?
questions.rationale: Both variables tend to increase together.

questions.prompt: A best-fit line is y = 2x + 5 for data with x-values from 1 to 8. Estimate y when x = 6.
questions.rationale: Substitute 6: 2 × 6 + 5 = 17.

parent_activity.prompt: Plot these paired values on squared paper: (1,2), (2,3), (3,3), (4,5), (5,4), (6,6), (7,6), (8,8), (9,7), (10,9). Label axes x and y, choose consistent scales, draw an estimated line of best fit, and use it to estimate y at x=5.
checklist: All ten points are placed against labelled axes with a consistent scale.
The line follows the overall positive trend with roughly balanced points above and below, rather than joining the dots.
The learner traces from x=5 to their line and reads a plausible y estimate, explaining that it is approximate.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks axis labeling, correlation, and a line-based estimate; it does not assess plotting points or drawing a best-fit line. Plotting and drawing a line of best fit require the parent-observed paper task; the quiz alone is partial.

lessons.explanation: Each scatter-graph point represents a pair of values. Positive correlation means both variables tend to rise together; negative means one tends to rise as the other falls. No correlation means no clear trend. A best-fit line summarizes a pattern and helps estimate values within the observed range.

worked_example.prompt: A best-fit line predicts 4 more sales for each 1°C increase. It predicts 20 sales at 10°C. What does it predict at 12°C?
steps: The temperature rises by 2°C, so sales rise by 2 × 4 = 8.
Add 8 to 20.

questions.prompt: When outdoor temperature rises, hot-chocolate sales tend to fall. What correlation is this?
questions.rationale: One variable tends to decrease as the other increases.

questions.prompt: A best-fit line is y = 3x + 2. Estimate y at x = 5, within the data range.
questions.rationale: Substitution gives 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.

questions.prompt: A scatter graph of shoe size and reading score has no clear upward or downward pattern. Which conclusion is best?
choices: There is no clear correlation in these data
Larger shoe sizes cause higher scores
Every point lies on a straight line
questions.rationale: A pattern without a trend indicates no clear correlation.

parent_activity.prompt: On graph paper, label x as study hours (0–5) and y as quiz score (0–10). Plot (1,2), (2,4), (3,5), (4,8), and (5,9). Describe the trend, draw a best-fit line, and use it to estimate the score at 3.5 study hours.
checklist: Labels both axes and plots all five pairs at the correct coordinates.
Describes the positive trend and draws a line through the general pattern.
Gives an estimate from the drawn line at 3.5 hours.

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz checks correlation meanings and prediction from a given line; the parent activity assesses plotting and drawing a best-fit line with supplied data.

lessons.explanation: A quarter is one of four equal parts of a whole. To find a quarter of a group, share its objects equally into four groups. Two quarters make a half. Split leftovers into equal pieces so everyone receives the same amount.

worked_example.prompt: Share 6 crackers equally among 4 friends. How many does each get?
steps: Give each friend 1 cracker; 2 remain.
Split each leftover into 4 equal pieces; give each friend one piece from each cracker.

questions.prompt: What is one quarter of 12 counters?
questions.rationale: Sharing 12 equally into 4 groups gives 3 in each.

questions.prompt: Five crackers are shared equally between 2 friends. How many does each get?
questions.rationale: Each gets 2 crackers and half of the leftover cracker.

questions.prompt: Five crackers are shared equally among 4 friends. How many does each get?
questions.rationale: Each gets 1 whole cracker and one quarter of the leftover.

parent_activity.prompt: Fold a paper shape into four equal parts. Name each part a quarter, compare it with a shape divided into four unequal parts, then show how two quarters make a half.
checklist: Identifies four equal parts as quarters.
Explains that four unequal parts are not quarters of the whole.
Shows that two quarters make a half.

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz checks quarter quantities and fair sharing; it does not assess folding or partitioning shapes, which the parent activity addresses.

lessons.explanation: Halves are two equal parts of one whole; fourths or quarters are four equal parts. The parts must be equal in size, not merely equal in number. Two halves joined make one whole, which helps solve sharing problems involving half-sandwiches.

worked_example.prompt: Four friends each need half a sandwich. How many whole sandwiches are needed?
steps: There are 4 half-sandwiches altogether.
Pair the halves: 2 halves make 1 whole, so 4 halves make 2 wholes.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is divided into 4 equal parts. What is each part called?
questions.rationale: Four equal parts are fourths, also called quarters.

questions.prompt: How many whole sandwiches are needed for 6 friends to each get half a sandwich?
questions.rationale: Six halves pair into three wholes.

questions.prompt: A circle is cut into 2 equal pieces. How many such pieces make 3 whole circles?
questions.rationale: Each circle has 2 halves, so 3 circles have 3 × 2 halves.

parent_activity.prompt: Fold paper circles and rectangles into equal shares, then label each share.
checklist: Shows a circle split into 2 equal halves
Shows a rectangle split into 4 equal quarters

lessons.coverage_note: Checks equal-share names and half-group reasoning; the paper task checks actual shape partitioning.

lessons.explanation: A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. The parts must be the same size. To find half of a group, share its objects equally into two groups; each group is half of the original amount.

worked_example.prompt: Find half of 8 counters.
steps: Share the 8 counters equally into 2 groups.
Each group has 8 ÷ 2 = 4 counters.

questions.prompt: What is half of 10 apples?
questions.rationale: Two equal groups of 5 make 10.

questions.prompt: A shape is split into two parts, one much larger than the other. Are the parts halves?
choices: Yes, any two parts are halves
Only if the shape is a circle
Yes, if both parts have straight edges
questions.rationale: Two parts are halves only when they are equal in size.

questions.prompt: A box has 18 crayons shared equally between 2 children. How many crayons does each get?
questions.rationale: Half of 18 is 18 ÷ 2 = 9.

parent_activity.prompt: Fold a paper shape into two equal parts and point to each half.
checklist: The fold makes two parts
The two parts are equal in size

lessons.coverage_note: Checks the meaning of equal halves and finding halves of quantities; it does not assess a range of shape partitions.

lessons.explanation: For unit fractions, the numerator is 1: more equal shares make each share smaller. With the same denominator, compare numerators because the pieces have equal size.

worked_example.prompt: Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/5 of the same pizza?
steps: Three shares are larger than five shares of the same whole.
So each third is larger than each fifth.

questions.prompt: Order 1/2, 1/4, and 1/6 from largest to smallest.
questions.rationale: More equal shares make each unit fraction smaller.

questions.prompt: Which is greater: 3/7 or 5/7?
questions.rationale: Both have sevenths; five sevenths is more than three sevenths.

questions.prompt: A sandwich is shared equally among 2, 3, or 8 people. Which person gets the smallest share?
questions.rationale: Eight equal shares make the smallest piece.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks unit fractions and same-denominator comparisons; it does not cover every fraction comparison method.

lessons.explanation: When the same whole is split into more equal pieces, each piece is smaller. The two halves are equal to each other, and the four quarters are equal to each other. A quarter is smaller than a half of the same whole.

worked_example.prompt: A 12 cm strip is split into 2 equal parts, then into 4 equal parts. How long is one part in each split?
steps: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm per half.
12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm per quarter.
worked_example.answer: A quarter is smaller: 3 cm instead of 6 cm.

questions.prompt: A 20 cm ribbon is cut into 4 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
questions.rationale: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm for each equal share.

questions.prompt: The same shape is divided into 2 equal pieces or 4 equal pieces. Which piece is smaller?
questions.rationale: Four equal shares are smaller than two equal shares of the same whole.

questions.prompt: A 24 cm strip is divided into equal pieces. Which cut makes each piece shorter: 3 equal pieces or 6 equal pieces?
questions.rationale: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm, less than 24 ÷ 3 = 8 cm.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check equal-share size with halves, quarters, and measured lengths; they do not assess drawing accuracy.

lessons.explanation: In a fraction, the denominator tells how many equal parts make a whole; the numerator tells how many parts are counted. A unit fraction has numerator 1; equivalent fractions name the same amount.

worked_example.prompt: In 2/4, name the numerator and denominator. Is it equivalent to 1/2?
steps: 2 is the numerator; 4 is the denominator.
Two of four equal parts is the same amount as one of two equal parts.

questions.prompt: In 3/5, what does the denominator 5 tell you?
choices: The whole is split into 5 equal parts
questions.rationale: The denominator names the number of equal parts in one whole.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
questions.rationale: Two of four equal parts make the same amount as one half.

questions.prompt: A recipe uses 7/4 cups of flour. Which description is correct?
questions.rationale: The numerator is greater than the denominator, so 7/4 is greater than one.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks numerator and denominator meanings, equivalence, and basic classification; not every listed term is tested.

lessons.explanation: A fraction of an amount means sharing it into equal parts, then taking the stated number of parts. To find 3/4 of a quantity, divide by 4 and multiply by 3. For a length, the same equal-part rule applies.

worked_example.prompt: Find 3/4 of 12 apples.
steps: Share 12 into 4 equal groups: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 apples per group.
Take 3 groups: 3 × 3 = 9 apples.

questions.prompt: A box has 15 counters. How many counters are 1/3 of the set?
questions.rationale: Sharing 15 counters into 3 equal groups gives 5 in each group.

questions.prompt: A 20 cm strip is split into 4 equal lengths. How long is 1/4 of the strip?
questions.rationale: Each quarter is one of 4 equal lengths: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm.

questions.prompt: A tray holds 24 buns. How many buns are 3/4 of the tray?
questions.rationale: One quarter is 24 ÷ 4 = 6; three quarters are 3 × 6 = 18.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check finding fractions of sets and lengths; they do not assess shading shapes or reading a ruler.

lessons.explanation: Halving splits something into two equal parts. Halve a whole once for halves, twice for quarters, and three times for eighths. Each extra halving splits every part in two, so 2 eighths cover the same amount as 1 quarter.

worked_example.prompt: A 16-minute activity is split into 8 equal parts. How long is one part?
steps: Divide 16 minutes by 8: each part is 2 minutes.
One of the 8 equal parts is one eighth of the activity.

questions.prompt: A 24-minute game is split into 8 equal time parts. How many minutes is one eighth?
questions.rationale: Each part is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 minutes.

questions.prompt: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. How many slices make one quarter of the pizza?
questions.rationale: One quarter is 2 of the 8 equal slices.

questions.prompt: A 40-minute activity is split into 8 equal parts. How many minutes are 3 eighths?
questions.rationale: One eighth is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 minutes; 3 parts last 15 minutes.

parent_activity.prompt: Fold a paper strip in half three times. Identify the halves, quarters, and eighths, and show that 2 eighths equal 1 quarter. Draw a 16-minute strip divided into 8 equal parts; label one part 1/8 and 2 minutes.
checklist: The folds show 2 halves, then 4 quarters, then 8 eighths.
The learner identifies 2 eighths as the same amount as 1 quarter.
The 16-minute strip has 8 equal parts, with one part labeled 1/8 and 2 minutes.

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz checks eighths in time and a pizza model. The activity also checks repeated halving and representing eighths; this is introductory practice, not a check of every fraction model.

lessons.explanation: Equal shares have the same area, even when their shapes look different. A whole split into 2 equal shares makes halves; into 3 makes thirds; into 4 makes fourths. Dividing lines must create parts of equal size, not merely parts that look similar.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 4 cm wide. Split it into 4 equal shares using vertical cuts. What is each share's area?
steps: The whole area is 8 × 4 = 32 square centimeters.
Divide 32 by 4 equal shares: each has area 8 square centimeters.
worked_example.answer: Each share has area 8 square centimeters.

questions.prompt: A circle is split into 3 equal slices. What is each slice called?
questions.rationale: Three equal shares of a whole are thirds.

questions.prompt: A 12 cm by 2 cm rectangle is split into 4 equal shares. What is the area of each share, in square centimeters?
questions.rationale: The area is 24 square centimeters, and 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

questions.prompt: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has area 24 square centimeters. Which share has the same area as one of 4 equal shares, even if it looks different?
choices: A triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm
A triangle with base 3 cm and height 4 cm
questions.rationale: One fourth is 6 square centimeters; the triangle's area is 3 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw a circle split into 3 equal shares, then draw a rectangle split into 4 equal shares in two different ways. Label the shares.
checklist: The circle has 3 equal-sized shares labeled thirds.
Each rectangle drawing has 4 equal-sized shares labeled fourths.
The two rectangle drawings may look different, but each share is one quarter of its whole.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks equal shares and area in circles and rectangles; it does not assess every possible partition.

lessons.explanation: A fraction names equal parts of a whole or a quantity. For a unit fraction such as 1/2, divide the quantity into 2 equal groups and take 1 group. Fractions can name the same amount: 2/4 equals 1/2 because two of four equal parts cover half the whole.

worked_example.prompt: Find 1/2 of 10.
steps: Divide 10 into 2 equal groups: 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
Take 1 group.

questions.prompt: What is 1/3 of 12?
questions.rationale: Divide 12 into 3 equal groups: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

questions.prompt: A strip is divided into 4 equal parts. Two parts are shaded. What fraction is shaded, and what is the same amount?
questions.rationale: Two of four equal parts are shaded, which is half the strip.

questions.prompt: A basket has 18 apples. You give away 2/3 of them. How many apples do you give away?
questions.rationale: One third is 18 ÷ 3 = 6; two thirds is 2 × 6 = 12.

parent_activity.prompt: Write equations for 1/2 of 10 and 1/3 of 12. Then draw a strip divided into 4 equal parts, shade 2, and use the drawing to explain why 2/4 = 1/2.
checklist: The equations show 1/2 of 10 = 5 and 1/3 of 12 = 4.
The strip has 4 equal parts, with exactly 2 shaded.
The explanation connects the 2 shaded parts out of 4 to half of the strip.

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz checks simple fractions of quantities and the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2. The activity checks writing equations and explaining equivalence with a drawing; general fraction operations are not covered.

lessons.explanation: To compare fractions, compare equal-sized parts or rewrite them with a common denominator. For a fraction of a quantity, divide by the denominator to find one part, then multiply by the numerator. Count tenths in steps of 0.1; a multi-step problem may use more than one of these ideas.

worked_example.prompt: A 20-liter tank is 3/5 full. How many liters are in it?
steps: One fifth is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 liters.
Three fifths is 3 × 4 = 12 liters.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is greater: 3/4 or 2/3?
questions.rationale: In twelfths, 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is 30 cm long. Mia uses 2/5 of it. How many centimeters does she use?
questions.rationale: One fifth is 30 ÷ 5 = 6 cm; two fifths is 12 cm.

questions.prompt: A jug contains 1/2 liter. You pour in 3/10 liter, then pour out 2/10 liter. How much remains?

lessons.coverage_note: This is a partial check of fraction comparison, quantities, tenths, and addition or subtraction in a short problem; it does not cover all fraction strategies.

lessons.explanation: Equivalent fractions name the same amount using different-sized equal parts. If each part is split into the same number of smaller equal parts, multiply both the numerator and denominator by that number. Splitting each half into 2 makes 2 fourths, so 1/2 = 2/4.

worked_example.prompt: A bar is half shaded. Each of its 2 equal parts is split into 2 equal smaller parts. What fraction of the 4 parts is shaded?
steps: The shaded half now contains 2 smaller parts.
There are 4 equal smaller parts altogether.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/3?
questions.rationale: Multiplying the numerator and denominator of 1/3 by 2 gives 2/6.

questions.prompt: A bar has 8 equal parts and 4 are shaded. Which fraction names the same shaded amount?
questions.rationale: Four of eight equal parts is half the bar.

questions.prompt: A 12 cm strip has 3 cm shaded. Which fraction of the strip is shaded?
questions.rationale: The shaded length is 3/12 of the strip, equivalent to 1/4.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw two equal-length bars. Divide one into 2 equal parts and shade 1; divide the other into 4 equal parts and shade 2. Compare the shaded lengths.
checklist: Both bars represent equal-sized wholes.
The first bar has 1 of 2 parts shaded and the second has 2 of 4.
The shaded lengths match, showing 1/2 = 2/4.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks small-denominator equivalence through part counts and lengths; it does not cover every equivalent fraction.

lessons.explanation: A fraction describes equal parts of one whole. In 1/b, the whole is divided into b equal parts and one part is named. In a/b, there are a parts, each the size of 1/b. The parts must be equal, and the whole must stay the same size.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangle is divided into 6 equal parts. What fraction is represented by 2 of those parts?
steps: The whole has 6 equal parts, so each part is 1/6.
Two parts are counted, each one sixth.

questions.prompt: A shape is divided into 5 equal parts. One part is shaded. What fraction is shaded?
questions.rationale: One of the 5 equal parts is shaded.

questions.prompt: A whole is divided into 4 equal parts. What does 3/4 mean?
questions.rationale: The denominator gives the size of each part; the numerator counts 3 parts.

questions.prompt: A strip is 18 cm long and divided into 6 equal parts. What length is 2/6 of the strip?
questions.rationale: Each sixth is 18 ÷ 6 = 3 cm; two sixths are 6 cm.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw a rectangle, divide it into 6 equal parts, and shade 2 parts. Label each part 1/6 and the shaded amount 2/6.
checklist: The rectangle is divided into 6 equal-sized parts.
Exactly 2 parts are shaded.
The labels show one part as 1/6 and the shaded amount as 2/6.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks how a fraction describes equal parts of a whole and simple part lengths; it does not cover fractions greater than one.

lessons.explanation: A number line shows fractions as positions between numbers. Divide the interval from 0 to 1 into equal steps: the denominator gives the number of steps, and the numerator tells how many steps from 0.

worked_example.prompt: Where is 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1?
steps: Divide the interval into 4 equal steps.
Count 3 steps from 0; the third mark is 3/4.
worked_example.answer: 3/4 is the third of four equal steps from 0.

questions.prompt: On a number line from 0 to 1, which point is halfway?
questions.rationale: Halfway divides the interval into two equal lengths.

questions.prompt: Which fraction lies between 0 and 1/2?
questions.rationale: One third is less than one half and greater than zero.

questions.prompt: The interval from 0 to 1 is divided into 8 equal steps. What fraction is at the fifth mark after 0?
questions.rationale: Five steps out of eight place the point at 5/8.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks positions between 0 and 1 with small denominators; it does not cover fractions beyond one.

lessons.explanation: When fractions have the same denominator, their pieces have equal size. Add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator; the result here stays within one whole.

worked_example.prompt: Calculate 2/5 + 2/5.
steps: Add the numerators: 2 + 2 = 4.
Keep the denominator 5.

questions.prompt: Calculate 3/8 + 2/8.
questions.rationale: Add the numerators and keep the denominator: 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.prompt: Calculate 7/9 − 4/9.
questions.rationale: Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: 7 − 4 = 3.

questions.prompt: A jug has 6/10 litre of juice. Someone pours out 3/10 litre. How much remains?
questions.rationale: Subtract equal-sized tenths: 6 − 3 = 3 tenths.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks addition and subtraction with the same denominator within one whole; unlike-denominator sums are not covered.

lessons.explanation: A tenth is one of 10 equal parts of a whole. Count tenths by adding or subtracting 0.1; 10 tenths make 1 whole. Dividing a number by 10 gives tenths when the number is a whole number below 10.

worked_example.prompt: Count up 3 tenths by 4 tenths.
steps: Start at 3 tenths.
Add 4 tenths: 7 tenths.

questions.prompt: A strip is split into 10 equal parts. What fraction is 6 parts?
questions.rationale: Six of the ten equal parts are selected.

questions.prompt: What is 4 ÷ 10, written as a fraction?
questions.rationale: Four divided into ten equal parts is four tenths.

questions.prompt: Count down by 1 tenth from 1 whole. What number do you reach?
questions.rationale: One whole is 10 tenths; one fewer is 9 tenths.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks tenths as equal parts, division by 10, and counting down; it does not assess every counting sequence.

lessons.explanation: To find a unit fraction of a set, divide the objects into as many equal groups as the denominator. To find several of those parts, multiply the amount in one group by the numerator.

worked_example.prompt: Find 3/4 of 12 buttons.
steps: Divide 12 buttons into 4 equal groups: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
Take 3 groups: 3 × 3 = 9.

questions.prompt: Find 1/4 of 12 counters.
questions.rationale: Dividing 12 counters into 4 equal groups gives 3 per group.

questions.prompt: Five of 8 stars are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
questions.rationale: Five of the eight stars are shaded.

questions.prompt: A tray has 18 grapes. Find 2/3 of the grapes.
questions.rationale: Each third is 6 grapes, so two thirds is 12.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks finding and naming fractions of sets with equal groups; it does not cover all denominators or more complex sets.

lessons.explanation: When denominators match, the fractions name equal-sized parts. Add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator. If the numerator is larger than the denominator, the result is greater than one whole.

worked_example.prompt: Calculate 3/5 + 4/5.
steps: Add the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7; keep the denominator 5.
7/5 is 1 whole and 2/5 left over.

questions.prompt: Calculate 2/7 + 3/7.
questions.rationale: Add the numerators and keep the denominator 7.

questions.prompt: Calculate 5/6 − 2/6.
questions.rationale: Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator 6.

questions.prompt: A ribbon piece is 7/8 m long and another is 3/8 m long. What is their total length?
questions.rationale: The total is 10/8 m, which is 1 2/8 m or 1 1/4 m.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks addition, subtraction, and a sum greater than one whole with like denominators; it does not assess unlike denominators.

lessons.explanation: For fractions with the same numerator, the larger denominator means smaller pieces. With the same denominator, compare numerators. Compare fractions only when they refer to equal-sized wholes.

worked_example.prompt: Compare 3/8 and 3/4 of equal-sized pizzas.
steps: Both fractions have numerator 3.
Eighths are smaller than fourths, so 3/8 < 3/4.

questions.prompt: Compare 5/6 and 2/6. Choose the correct comparison.
questions.rationale: The sixths are equal-sized, and five parts are more than two.

questions.prompt: Two equal-sized cakes are divided into 5 and 8 equal pieces. Compare 1/5 and 1/8.
questions.rationale: Fifths are larger pieces than eighths of the same-sized whole.

questions.prompt: Two equal-sized garden beds are divided into equal parts. Compare 4/7 of one bed with 4/9 of the other.
questions.rationale: The wholes match; sevenths are larger pieces than ninths.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks comparisons with a shared numerator or denominator when the wholes are equal-sized; it does not cover general comparisons with unlike numerators and denominators.

lessons.explanation: A fraction with denominator 10 gives tenths, written with one digit after the decimal point. A denominator of 100 gives hundredths, written with two digits after the decimal point; keep a zero when needed.

worked_example.prompt: Write 45/100 as a decimal.
steps: The denominator is 100, so use two decimal places.
45 hundredths is 0.45.

questions.prompt: Write 7/10 as a decimal.
questions.rationale: Seven tenths is written with 7 in the tenths place.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equal to 0.32?
questions.rationale: The digits represent 32 hundredths.

questions.prompt: A measuring cup contains 6/10 litre. A mark is at 0.60 litre. Are these amounts equal?
questions.rationale: Six tenths equals sixty hundredths, or 0.60.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks decimal equivalents in tenths and hundredths, including a trailing zero; it does not cover every decimal place.

lessons.explanation: Decimal places show tenths, hundredths, then thousandths. Per cent means out of 100, and % is its symbol. Fractions, decimals, and percentages can name the same value, such as 1/2, 0.5, and 50%.

worked_example.prompt: Convert 3/4 to a decimal and percentage.
steps: 3/4 = 75/100, so the decimal is 0.75.
75 out of 100 is 75%.

questions.prompt: In 4.27, what is the value of the digit 2?
questions.rationale: The 2 is in the tenths place.

questions.prompt: Which expression means 35 out of 100?
questions.rationale: The percent symbol means out of 100.

questions.prompt: A bottle is 0.6 full. Which fraction and percentage show the same amount?
questions.rationale: 0.6 equals 6/10, or 60/100, which is 3/5 and 60%.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks place value, percent notation, and a simple fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence; it does not cover all conversions or thousandths.

lessons.explanation: To round a decimal with one digit after the decimal point to the nearest whole number, look at the tenths digit. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, round down.

worked_example.prompt: Round 6.5 to the nearest whole number.
steps: The tenths digit is 5.
Round up from 6 to 7.

questions.prompt: Round 3.2 to the nearest whole number.
questions.rationale: The tenths digit is 2, so round down to 3.

questions.prompt: Round 8.7 to the nearest whole number.
questions.rationale: The tenths digit is 7, so round up to 9.

questions.prompt: A length is 12.5 cm. Rounded to the nearest whole centimetre, what is it?
questions.rationale: The tenths digit is 5, so round up to 13 cm.

lessons.coverage_note: This short quiz checks rounding one-decimal-place numbers to whole numbers; it does not cover other decimal places.

lessons.explanation: Compare whole-number parts first. If they are equal, compare tenths, then hundredths. The first place where the digits differ tells which number is larger.

worked_example.prompt: Which is greater, 3.72 or 3.27?
steps: Both have 3 ones; compare tenths: 7 is greater than 2.
So 3.72 is greater than 3.27.

questions.prompt: Which number is smallest: 0.45, 0.54, or 0.39?
questions.rationale: The tenths digits are 4, 5, and 3; 3 is smallest.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct comparison.
questions.rationale: The tenths digits match; 8 hundredths is greater than 2.

questions.prompt: Put these in order from smallest to largest: 2.08, 2.80, 2.18.
questions.rationale: The ones match; compare tenths, then hundredths: 08, 18, 80.

lessons.coverage_note: This short quiz checks comparisons and ordering for decimals with the same number of decimal places, up to two places.

lessons.explanation: For money and measures, convert fractions to useful amounts or subtract decimals by aligning decimal points. Keep units attached to the answer; 1 kg equals 1,000 g.

worked_example.prompt: A rope is 2.5 m long. How much remains after cutting off 0.75 m?
steps: Write 2.5 as 2.50 to align hundredths.

questions.prompt: What is 1/4 of £3.20?
questions.rationale: One quarter is one of four equal parts: £3.20 ÷ 4 = £0.80.

questions.prompt: A 4.6 m ribbon has 1.25 m cut off. How much remains?
Find 3/10 of 2 kg. Give the amount in grams and as a decimal of a kilogram.
questions.rationale: 3/10 of 2 kg is 0.6 kg, and 0.6 kg is 600 g.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions sample fraction-of-money and decimal-measure problems; they do not cover every unit conversion.

lessons.explanation: Dividing by 10 moves each digit one place to a smaller value column; dividing by 100 moves it two places. A digit in the ones place becomes tenths after dividing by 10, or hundredths after dividing by 100. Use place value to read the result.

worked_example.prompt: Calculate 37 ÷ 10 and name the value of each digit.
steps: Move each digit one place to a smaller column: 3 tens become 3 ones; 7 ones become 7 tenths.
worked_example.answer: 3.7; 3 is in the ones place and 7 is in the tenths place.

questions.prompt: What is 46 ÷ 10?
questions.rationale: Dividing by 10 shifts each digit one place to the right in the place-value chart.

questions.prompt: In 8 ÷ 100 = 0.08, what place is the 8 in?
questions.rationale: Dividing 8 by 100 gives 0.08, where 8 represents eight hundredths.

questions.prompt: A 53 cm ribbon is cut into 100 equal parts. How long is each part in centimetres?
questions.rationale: Each part is 53 ÷ 100 = 0.53 cm? Check place value: 53 hundredths is 0.53 cm.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check division by 10 and 100 and place value; they do not cover every way to represent decimals.

lessons.explanation: Equivalent fractions name the same-sized amount. Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number to make an equivalent fraction; the equal-sized parts change, but the total amount does not.

steps: To change 4 to 8, multiply by 2; multiply 1 by 2 to get 2.
To change 4 to 12, multiply by 3; multiply 1 by 3 to get 3.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/3?
questions.rationale: Multiplying both 1 and 3 by 2 gives 2/6.

questions.prompt: Simplify 4/8 by dividing the numerator and denominator by 4.
A strip has 12 equal parts, and 9 are shaded. Which fraction names the same amount using 4 equal parts?
questions.rationale: Divide 9 and 12 by 3: 9/12 = 3/4.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw one rectangle, shade 1/3, then divide each third into two equal parts. Compare the shaded area before and after the extra lines.
checklist: Shows 1 of 3 equal regions shaded before subdivision.
Shows 2 of 6 equal regions shaded afterward.
Explains that the shaded area stays the same.

lessons.coverage_note: The questions check generating and simplifying simple equivalents; the drawing activity checks the area-model explanation.

lessons.explanation: Fractions are equivalent when they mark the same point between 0 and 1. To check, split the whole into equal parts and compare the distance from 0; multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number preserves that point.

worked_example.prompt: Do 2/3 and 4/6 mark the same point?
steps: Divide the whole into 3 equal lengths: 2/3 is two lengths from 0.
Divide into 6 equal lengths: 4/6 is four lengths from 0; both are 2/3 of the whole.

questions.prompt: Which fraction marks the same point as 1/2 on a number line from 0 to 1?
questions.rationale: Two of four equal intervals reach the midpoint.

questions.prompt: Which set contains three fractions that all mark the midpoint from 0 to 1?
questions.rationale: Each fraction equals one half, so each lands at the midpoint.

questions.prompt: A path from 0 to 1 is divided into 12 equal steps. Which fraction reaches the same point as 3/4?
questions.rationale: Multiply the numerator and denominator of 3/4 by 3: 9/12.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Mark 1/2, 2/4, and 3/6 using their own equal subdivisions, then compare the marks.
checklist: Marks the interval from 0 to 1 and divides it into equal parts for each fraction.
Places each fraction at the midpoint.
Explains that matching positions show equal values.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check common equivalent fractions and their shared number-line position; the drawing activity checks placement directly.

lessons.explanation: A fraction names equal parts of one whole. To change these fractions to decimals, write them in hundredths: 1/2=50/100=0.50, 1/4=25/100=0.25, and 3/4=75/100=0.75.

worked_example.prompt: Write 3/4 as a decimal.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by 25: 3/4=75/100.
Hundredths are two decimal places: 75/100=0.75.

questions.prompt: Which decimal equals 1/4?
questions.rationale: One quarter is 25 hundredths, or 0.25.

questions.prompt: A hundredths grid has 50 of its 100 squares shaded. What fraction and decimal describe the shaded part? Choose the decimal.
questions.rationale: 50/100 simplifies to 1/2, which is 0.5.

questions.prompt: A strip is divided into 4 equal parts, and 3 parts are shaded. What decimal of the strip is shaded?
questions.rationale: Three quarters is 75 hundredths, or 0.75.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks the three named fraction-decimal equivalents, but not broad decimal conversion.

lessons.explanation: A unit fraction names one of several equal-area parts. If a whole is split into 6 equal-area pieces, each piece is 1/6 of the whole. The pieces may have different shapes, but their areas must be equal.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangle is split into 6 equal-area pieces. What fraction of the rectangle is one piece?
steps: Count 6 equal parts in the whole.
One part out of 6 is 1/6.

questions.prompt: A square is split into 4 equal-area parts. What fraction of the square is one part?
questions.rationale: One of four equal parts is 1/4 of the whole.

questions.prompt: A cake is cut into 8 equal-area slices. What fraction of the whole cake is one slice?
questions.rationale: One slice is one of the 8 equal parts.

questions.prompt: A rectangle has area 24 square centimetres and is partitioned into 6 equal-area pieces. What is the area of one piece?
questions.rationale: Each equal piece has area 24/6=4 square centimetres.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw a square and partition it in two different ways into 4 equal-area parts. Label one part in each drawing.
checklist: Each drawing shows 4 parts covering the whole square.
The parts in each drawing have equal area.
One part is labelled 1/4 in each drawing.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks unit fractions and equal-area partitioning; it does not assess a wide range of shapes.

lessons.explanation: A fraction such as 5/8 means five copies of the unit fraction 1/8. Keep the denominator because each step is one eighth; count the numerator’s number of steps.

worked_example.prompt: Write 4/3 as a sum of unit fractions.
steps: The denominator 3 gives the unit fraction 1/3.
