parent_activity.prompt: Choose a pencil and a book. Name measurable attributes of each. Align their ends to compare lengths, then carefully lift each to compare weights.
checklist: Names length and weight as measurable attributes of both objects.
Aligns starting ends before comparing lengths.
Correctly describes the objects as longer, shorter, heavier, lighter, or equal based on the comparisons.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions partially check identifying attributes and comparing stated measurements. The activity provides observable comparison practice; the quiz does not assess hands-on measuring or capacity testing.

lessons.explanation: Compare two objects by holding them or with a balance. Say heavier than or lighter than. The lower side is heavier. The higher side is lighter.

worked_example.prompt: A balance has a book on the left and a pencil on the right. The left side goes down. Which object is heavier?
steps: The side that goes down is heavier.
The book is on the left, so the book is heavier than the pencil.
worked_example.answer: The book is heavier than the pencil.

questions.prompt: You hold a full water bottle and an empty cup. The bottle pulls down more. Which sentence is true?
choices: The empty cup is heavier than the bottle.
The bottle is heavier than the empty cup.
Both objects have the same weight.
The empty cup feels heavy and the bottle feels light.
questions.rationale: The hand pulled down more holds the heavier object.

questions.prompt: A balance has an apple on the left and a grape on the right. The grape side goes up. Which object is lighter?
choices: The apple is lighter than the grape.
The apple and the grape weigh the same.
The grape is lighter than the apple.
The apple goes up, so the apple is light.
questions.rationale: The side that rises is lighter, and the grape is on that side.

questions.prompt: One balance puts a rock lower than a block. Another puts the block lower than a sponge. Which list is heaviest to lightest?
questions.rationale: The lower object is heavier: rock, then block, then sponge.

parent_activity.prompt: Hold two safe household objects, one in each hand. Then set them on opposite ends of a simple balance. Say which is heavier and which is lighter.
checklist: Names the object that felt heavier when held.
Points to the balance side that went down as heavier.
Says a sentence using heavier than or lighter than.

lessons.coverage_note: These items check heavier and lighter comparisons from stated results only. A real hold or balance is still needed. Scale numbers and units are not covered.

lessons.explanation: Time words order events. First is earliest, next comes after, and last is latest. Yesterday is before today. Tomorrow is after today. Morning comes before afternoon, then evening.

worked_example.prompt: This morning you eat cereal, then walk the dog, then go to class. What is first, next, and last?
steps: Cereal starts the morning, so it is first.
The dog walk is next, and class is last.
worked_example.answer: First cereal, next the dog walk, last class.

questions.prompt: You wake up, then brush teeth, then eat toast. What happens next after waking?
questions.rationale: Brushing comes right after waking and before toast.

questions.prompt: You baked muffins yesterday. You read a book today. The day after today you will swim. Which event happens tomorrow?
questions.rationale: Tomorrow means the day after today, when you swim.

questions.prompt: Yesterday afternoon was a picnic. This morning is reading. This evening is a bath. Tomorrow morning is a walk. Which event is last?
questions.rationale: Tomorrow comes after today, so the walk is later than this evening.

parent_activity.prompt: Name three things done today and put them in order with first, next, and last. Add one yesterday event and one tomorrow plan. Tell if each was morning, afternoon, or evening.
checklist: Orders three today events as first, next, and last to match the real day.
Puts the yesterday event before today and the tomorrow plan after today.
Labels each event morning, afternoon, or evening to match when it happens.

lessons.coverage_note: Partial check of time-order words with events already given. It does not show a child can sequence a full real day alone.

lessons.explanation: Capacity is how much a container can hold. Measure it with equal full cups or litres. Count carefully, then record both the number and the unit.

worked_example.prompt: An empty bucket fills exactly with two full 1-litre jugs. What is its capacity?
steps: Count 1 litre for each full jug.
Add the amounts: 1 + 1 = 2 litres.

questions.prompt: You pour 2 full cups into an empty jug, then 3 more to fill it exactly. Every cup holds the same amount. What is the jug’s capacity in cups?
questions.rationale: Count every cup poured: 2 + 3 = 5 cups.

questions.prompt: Three full 1-litre bottles fill an empty bowl exactly. Which record gives its capacity with the correct number and unit?
questions.rationale: Each bottle holds 1 litre, so three bottles measure 3 litres.

questions.prompt: An empty container receives 2 litres, then 1 litre, then another 2 litres. It is now exactly full, with nothing spilled. What is its capacity in litres?
questions.rationale: Add all three amounts: 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 litres.

parent_activity.prompt: With an adult, measure a small container using one cup repeatedly. Then measure a larger container using a marked litre jug. Record each capacity; use a partial final measure if needed.
checklist: Uses equal full cups and notes any partly filled final cup.
Reads the litre jug’s markings and counts all amounts poured.
Writes each measured capacity with its unit: cups or litres.

lessons.coverage_note: These quizzes partially check counting measured amounts and recording units. The hands-on activity checks actual filling, reading markings, and recording; quizzes alone cannot assess measurement technique.

lessons.explanation: Coins: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2. Notes: £5 and £10. £1 equals 100p. Compare values, not sizes.

worked_example.prompt: Which is worth more: a £2 coin or a 50p coin?
steps: £2 equals 200p.
200p is more than 50p.

questions.prompt: Which coin is worth more than a 50p coin?
questions.rationale: £2 equals 200p, which is more than 50p.

questions.prompt: Which is worth more than a £5 note?
questions.rationale: £10 is more than £5. Each listed coin is worth less than £5.

questions.prompt: Which list puts these coins in order from least to greatest value?
questions.rationale: The values are 1p, 5p, 20p and 100p, increasing in that order.

parent_activity.prompt: With an adult, examine real or play versions of all eight listed coins and £5 and £10 notes. Name their values, then arrange them from least to greatest.
checklist: Identifies each coin by its value, using its markings.
Distinguishes the £5 note from the £10 note.
Orders the money correctly, placing £2 above 50p.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions partially check coin and note value comparisons and coin ordering. Recognising every physical coin and note needs the hands-on activity.

lessons.explanation: A week has seven days in order. A year has twelve months in order; it is about 52 weeks long, though months do not all contain the same number of weeks.

worked_example.prompt: What day is two days after Tuesday?
steps: Count one day: Wednesday.
Count a second day: Thursday.

questions.prompt: Which day comes immediately after Saturday?
questions.rationale: Sunday follows Saturday in the seven-day week.

questions.prompt: Which month comes immediately before October?
questions.rationale: September is the ninth month; October is the tenth.

questions.prompt: A date is in February. Which month will come two months later?
questions.rationale: Count forward: March, then April.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check day and month order, not calendar reading, leap years, or the exact length of every month.

lessons.explanation: A minute contains 60 seconds. Use a timer to measure how long an activity takes, then record the duration with a number and unit, such as 45 seconds or 2 minutes.

worked_example.prompt: A timer runs for 1 minute and then 15 more seconds. How long is that altogether?
steps: Convert 1 minute to 60 seconds.
Add 15 seconds: 60 + 15 = 75 seconds.

questions.prompt: How many seconds are in 1 minute?
questions.rationale: One minute is made up of 60 seconds.

questions.prompt: A short activity takes 40 seconds. Which record matches its duration?
questions.rationale: The number and unit match the measured duration.

questions.prompt: A timer shows 60 seconds, then runs 20 more seconds. What is the total duration in seconds?
questions.rationale: Add the extra 20 seconds to 60 seconds: 80 seconds.

parent_activity.prompt: Choose a safe, brief activity such as stacking five blocks. Time it with a stopwatch, repeat once, and record both durations.
checklist: Uses a timer to measure each attempt
Records each result with a number and seconds or minutes
Compares the two recorded durations

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check the 60-second relationship and simple duration recording; hands-on timing is needed to practise measuring.

lessons.explanation: Measure from the object’s starting edge and record the number with its unit. Cubes can give a non-standard length; a ruler gives centimetres. Line up the ruler’s zero mark with the edge before reading.

worked_example.prompt: A ribbon starts at 0 cm and ends at 8 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
steps: Check that the ribbon starts at the ruler’s 0 cm mark.
Read the ending mark: 8 cm.

questions.prompt: A desk is 7 cubes long when cubes are placed end to end. How should you record its length?
questions.rationale: The desk was measured using cubes, so record that unit.

questions.prompt: A pencil begins at 0 cm and ends at 12 cm on a ruler. How long is it?
questions.rationale: The length is the ending mark minus zero: 12 cm.

questions.prompt: A strip begins at 3 cm and ends at 11 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
questions.rationale: Subtract the starting mark: 11 − 3 = 8 cm.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure a table first with identical cubes placed end to end, then with a ruler. Record both measurements and their units.
checklist: Places cubes end to end without gaps or overlaps
Lines the ruler’s zero mark up with the table edge
Records each result with the correct unit

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check unit choice and reading simple ruler measurements; actual measuring and recording need hands-on practice.

lessons.explanation: A balance compares mass: the lower side has greater mass. You can also measure using equal units, such as cubes, or read a scale. Record both the number and unit, such as 5 cubes or 300 g.

worked_example.prompt: A book balances with 6 identical cubes. What is its mass in cube units?
steps: Count the cubes used to balance the book: 6.
Record the count with its unit.

questions.prompt: On a balance, the left pan with a ball hangs lower than the right pan with a toy. Which has greater mass?
questions.rationale: The lower side of a balance has greater mass.

questions.prompt: A bag balances with 5 identical cubes. Which record matches the measurement?
questions.rationale: Cubes were the units used to measure the bag’s mass.

questions.prompt: A scale’s pointer is exactly on 300 g. How should you record the mass?
questions.rationale: The pointer gives 300, and the scale unit is grams.

parent_activity.prompt: With an adult, compare two safe objects on a balance, then find how many identical cubes balance one object. Record the result.
checklist: Identifies the lower side as having greater mass
Uses identical cubes as units
Records the count with the unit cubes

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check balance comparisons and simple mass records; using a real balance or scale is needed to practise measuring.

lessons.explanation: On an analogue clock, the minute hand points to 12 at an hour and to 6 at half past. At half past, the hour hand sits halfway between that hour’s number and the next. Digital time writes half past as :30.

worked_example.prompt: Show half past 2 on an analogue clock. What digital time is it?
steps: Put the minute hand on 6 for 30 minutes.
Put the hour hand halfway between 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: What is half past 7 in digital time?
questions.rationale: Half past means 30 minutes after the hour.

questions.prompt: A digital clock shows 3:00. Where is the minute hand on an analogue clock?
questions.rationale: At an exact hour, the minute hand points to 12.

questions.prompt: Which clock description shows half past 4?
choices: Minute hand on 12; hour hand on 4
Minute hand on 6; hour hand halfway between 4 and 5
Minute hand on 4; hour hand on 6
Minute hand on 6; hour hand on 5
questions.rationale: Half past has the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand between 4 and 5.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw clock faces for 3:00 and half past 2. Add both hands, then write each digital time beside its clock.
checklist: Places the minute hand on 12 for 3:00
Places the minute hand on 6 for half past 2
Places the half-past hour hand between 2 and 3

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check hour and half-hour reading; drawing accurate clock hands needs a clock face or drawing activity.

lessons.explanation: Different coin groups can have the same value. Add each coin’s value to check a group. To find a combination, choose coins for part of the total, then make the remainder.

worked_example.prompt: Two 20p coins are part of a 50p total. What coin completes it?

questions.prompt: What is the total value in pence of two 20p coins and one 10p coin?
questions.rationale: Two 20p coins and one 10p coin total 50p.

questions.prompt: How many 10p coins equal the value of one 50p coin?
questions.rationale: Five 10p coins total 50p.

questions.prompt: You have two 20p coins and want exactly 60p. What value must the additional coin have?
questions.rationale: The coins total 40p, leaving 20p to reach 60p.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check adding coin values and finding matching combinations; they do not cover every possible coin set or require systematic listing of all combinations.

lessons.explanation: Area counts the square units covering a flat shape, with no gaps or overlaps. For an L shape, count each row, then add the row totals. Write square centimetres as cm².

worked_example.prompt: An L shape has 5 unit squares in its top row and 2 in each of its next 2 rows. What is its area?
steps: Count: 5 + 2 + 2.
Add: 9 unit squares.

questions.prompt: A book cover is covered by 4 rows of 6 square-centimetre tiles. What is its area in cm²?
questions.rationale: There are 4 rows of 6 tiles: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.prompt: Shape A has 7 unit squares. Shape B has 3 rows of 3 unit squares. Which has greater area?
questions.rationale: Shape B covers 9 squares, more than Shape A's 7.

questions.prompt: A floor shape has rows of 8, 3, and 3 square tiles. What is its area in square metres if each tile is 1 m²?
questions.rationale: Add all the tiles: 8 + 3 + 3 = 14.

parent_activity.prompt: Cover a flat book or box lid with identical 1 cm² tiles, then count the tiles. Keep tiles aligned without gaps or overlaps.
checklist: Tiles cover the surface without gaps or overlaps
Counts tiles in rows and adds the row totals

lessons.coverage_note: Checks counting and comparing square units on simple shapes; it does not cover irregular units or area formulas.

lessons.explanation: Choose units that fit the quantity: centimetres or metres for length, grams or kilograms for mass, millilitres or litres for capacity, and degrees Celsius for temperature. Measure with the matching tool and record to a sensible unit.

worked_example.prompt: A table measures 120 cm. How many metres is that?

questions.prompt: Which unit is most suitable for measuring the length of a classroom table?
questions.rationale: Centimetres measure length at a useful scale for a table.

questions.prompt: A bag of flour has a mass of 2 kg. How many grams is that?
questions.rationale: 1 kg is 1000 g, so 2 kg is 2000 g.

questions.prompt: A jug contains 750 ml of juice. How many more millilitres are needed to reach 1 litre?

parent_activity.prompt: Measure a table with a ruler or tape, weigh a small object on a scale, and read the amount in a measuring jug. Record each value with its unit.
checklist: Uses a suitable unit for each quantity
Reads and records each measuring tool accurately

lessons.coverage_note: Practises choosing units and converting simple metric measures; it does not assess temperature readings or rounding from real instruments.

lessons.explanation: To compare measurements, first use the same unit. Then compare the numbers and write > for greater than, < for less than, or = for equal to.

worked_example.prompt: Compare 1 m and 85 cm.
steps: Convert 1 m to 100 cm.
Since 100 cm is greater than 85 cm, write 1 m > 85 cm.

questions.prompt: Choose the true comparison.
questions.rationale: 45 is greater than 32, so the correct symbol is >.

questions.prompt: Order these capacities from least to greatest: 1 L, 600 ml, 900 ml.
A parcel has a mass of 1 kg. Compare it with a 950 g parcel.
questions.rationale: 1 kg is 1000 g, which is greater than 950 g.

parent_activity.prompt: Choose two household objects and compare their lengths, then compare two containers' measured capacities. Record each pair using >, <, or = after checking units match.
checklist: Uses matching units before comparing
Writes the correct comparison symbol for both pairs

lessons.coverage_note: Checks comparisons and ordering of simple metric measurements; it does not cover conversions between all units or measurement uncertainty.

lessons.explanation: Compare mass by weighing objects on the same balance, or compare capacity by filling each container and pouring it separately into the same empty jug. If A is heavier than B and B heavier than C, A is heavier than C.

worked_example.prompt: A balance shows an apple is heavier than a block, and the block is heavier than an egg. Which is heavier, the apple or egg?
steps: The apple is heavier than the block.
The block is heavier than the egg, so the apple is heavier than the egg.
worked_example.answer: The apple is heavier than the egg.

questions.prompt: On a balance, a pear is heavier than a toy. The toy is heavier than a plum. What follows?
choices: The plum is heavier than the pear
The pear is heavier than the plum
The pear and plum have equal mass
The toy is lighter than the plum
questions.rationale: The pear outweighs the toy, which outweighs the plum.

questions.prompt: Each bottle is filled to capacity, then poured separately into the same empty jug. A reaches 700 ml; B reaches 500 ml. Which held more?
choices: The jug determines which held more
questions.rationale: The same jug shows A held 200 ml more than B.

questions.prompt: Using the same level cup, it takes 5 cups to fill a bowl, 3 to fill a jar, and 2 to fill a tin. Order capacities from greatest to least.
questions.rationale: More equal cups fit in the bowl, then the jar, then the tin.

parent_activity.prompt: Compare two objects on a balance. Then fill each of two containers to capacity and pour each separately into the same initially empty jug, emptying it between trials. Explain what the results show.
checklist: Uses the same balance for both objects and compares the result
Fills each container to capacity and empties the jug between pours
Explains which object is heavier or which container holds more, based on observations

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz partially checks reasoning from supplied comparisons; the parent activity checks hands-on balance and jug use and explaining observed results.

lessons.explanation: Capacity is how much a container can hold when full; volume is how much liquid is in it now. Estimate by comparing with a familiar cup or measure, then fill and check using equal measures.

worked_example.prompt: A 1-litre jug is half full. What is its capacity, and how much liquid is in it?
steps: It can hold 1 litre, so its capacity is 1 litre.
Half of 1 litre is 500 ml, the amount it holds now.

questions.prompt: A mug is about the size of a 300 ml measuring cup. Which is a reasonable capacity estimate?
questions.rationale: A similar-sized mug is reasonably estimated at about 300 ml.

questions.prompt: A 1-litre jug is half full of water. How much water is in the jug?
questions.rationale: Half of 1 litre, or 1000 ml, is 500 ml.

questions.prompt: A container holds 4 equal cups when full. It currently holds 3 cups. What are its capacity and current volume?
questions.rationale: Capacity is the full 4 cups; the current amount is 3 cups.

parent_activity.prompt: Estimate a container’s capacity using a familiar cup or 1-litre bottle. Fill it with equal measures, count them, and compare the result with your estimate.
checklist: States an estimate before filling
Uses equal measures and records the checked capacity

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz checks selection of a reasonable capacity estimate and capacity versus current liquid volume. Actual estimation and checking by filling are assessed only through the parent activity.

lessons.explanation: Estimate length by comparing with a known reference, such as a 10 cm ruler or a paper clip. Then measure with equal units or a ruler and compare your estimate with the result.

worked_example.prompt: A pencil looks about three times as long as a 10 cm ruler. Estimate its length.
steps: Use the known length: 3 × 10 cm.
The estimate is 30 cm.

questions.prompt: A ribbon looks about twice as long as a 15 cm ruler. What is a reasonable estimate?
questions.rationale: Twice 15 cm is 30 cm.

questions.prompt: A paper clip is about 3 cm long. A line looks about 5 paper clips long. Estimate the line's length.
questions.rationale: Five lengths of about 3 cm give 15 cm.

questions.prompt: You estimate a stick is 40 cm. A ruler check gives 46 cm. How far off was your estimate?
questions.rationale: The difference is 46 − 40 = 6 cm.

parent_activity.prompt: Pick a household object, estimate its length using a familiar reference, then measure it with a ruler or equal units. Record both lengths and how far apart they are.
checklist: Makes and records an estimate before measuring
Measures with a ruler or equal units
Records the difference between estimate and measurement

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz partially checks calculations from supplied references and measurements; only the parent activity checks independently estimating before measuring and physically measuring.

lessons.explanation: Compare lengths from matching starting points. Order objects from shortest to longest. A string can carry a length between objects. If A is longer than B and B than C, A is longer than C.

worked_example.prompt: Red ribbon is 7 cm long, blue is 4 cm, and yellow is 9 cm. Order them shortest to longest.
steps: Compare lengths: 4 cm is shorter than 7 cm.
Compare again: 7 cm is shorter than 9 cm.

questions.prompt: Three sticks measure: oak 8 cm, pine 3 cm, birch 5 cm. Which order goes from shortest to longest?
questions.rationale: 3 cm is less than 5 cm, which is less than 8 cm.

questions.prompt: A string exactly matches a red box's height. Held straight from the blue box's bottom, it ends below the blue box's top. Which box is taller?
questions.rationale: The blue box is taller than the string, and the string matches the red box.

questions.prompt: Tower A is taller than a straight string. Tower B is shorter than that string. Tower C is taller than Tower A. Which tower is shortest?
questions.rationale: B is shorter than the string, which is shorter than A. C is taller than A, so B is shortest.

parent_activity.prompt: Provide three unequal ribbons and two boxes kept apart. Have the learner order the ribbons, then compare box heights using a nonstretchy string without moving the boxes together.
checklist: Aligns ribbon ends and orders all three shortest to longest.
Marks one box's height on the string and compares that same marked length with the other box from its bottom.
Explains how the string comparison shows which box is taller.

lessons.coverage_note: These quizzes partially check ordering and indirect comparisons from stated facts. The activity checks physical alignment, string use, and an explanation; choices alone cannot assess those actions.

lessons.explanation: Use equal-size units to measure length. Start at one end and place units touching, without gaps or overlaps. Count every unit needed to reach the other end.

worked_example.prompt: A book's edge fits exactly 5 equal paper clips. How do you measure it?
steps: Place 3 clips end to end from one corner, then add 2 more to reach the other corner.
Check for gaps or overlaps, then count: 3 + 2 = 5.
worked_example.answer: The book's edge is 5 paper-clip lengths.

questions.prompt: A ribbon fits exactly 2 silver clips and 3 gold clips, all the same size, touching end to end without overlaps. How many clip-lengths long is it?
questions.rationale: Color does not change the unit size. Count all the clips: 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement correctly measures a pencil from one end to the other?
choices: Equal clips with spaces between them
Different-size clips touching end to end
Equal clips touching end to end without overlaps
questions.rationale: Equal units must cover the whole length without gaps or overlaps.

questions.prompt: A strip is exactly 7 clip-lengths long. You have only 4 equal clips. After placing all 4, you mark their endpoint and move clips forward from that mark. How many more clip placements finish measuring the strip?
questions.rationale: Four unit-lengths are already measured. Another 7 − 4 = 3 placements reach the end without gaps or overlaps.

parent_activity.prompt: Together, choose a book edge. Lay equal-size paper clips along it. If the endpoint falls between clips, report that honestly rather than rounding to a whole clip.
checklist: Starts the first clip at one end and uses equal-size clips.
Places clips end to end without gaps or overlaps.
Counts the clips and states either an exact length or that the endpoint falls between whole units.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions partially check unit counting, placement rules, and reusing units. The activity checks actual measuring; multiple choice alone cannot show careful placement.

lessons.explanation: Add pence prices to find a total. Subtract to find change from a coin, or how many more pence you still need.

worked_example.prompt: A pencil costs 20p and a rubber costs 15p. What is the total cost in pence?
steps: Add the two prices: 20 + 15.
20 + 15 = 35, so the total is 35p.

questions.prompt: A pen costs 25p and an eraser costs 14p. What is the total cost in pence?
questions.rationale: Adding 25 and 14 gives 39.

questions.prompt: You pay with 50p for an item costing 35p. How much change, in pence, do you get?
questions.rationale: Subtract 35 from 50 to get 15.

questions.prompt: A toy costs 36p and a book costs 27p. You have 50p. How many more pence do you need?
questions.rationale: The items cost 63p, and 63 minus 50 is 13.

lessons.coverage_note: Practice checks two-price totals, change from 50p, and how much more is needed. It does not cover pounds or longer shopping lists.

lessons.explanation: A currency’s main unit is split into 100 smaller units: £1 = 100p or $1 = 100c. The symbol identifies the currency. To combine amounts, write them in the same unit, then add.

worked_example.prompt: How many pence are in £2.35?

questions.prompt: How many cents are in $4.08?
questions.rationale: Four dollars are 400 cents; add 8 cents.

questions.prompt: Which coin amounts total 85p?
A snack costs £1.45. You pay with 100p, 20p, 20p, and 5p. How much do you pay in pounds?
questions.rationale: The coins total 145p, which is £1.45.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks unit conversion, reading prices, and combining amounts; it does not cover every currency or coin system.

lessons.explanation: One hour has 60 minutes. One day has 24 hours. Use these facts to convert: multiply hours by 60 to get minutes, or divide minutes by 60 to get hours.

worked_example.prompt: How many minutes are in 3 hours?
steps: There are 60 minutes in each hour.
3 × 60 = 180 minutes.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are in 2 hours?
questions.rationale: Two groups of 60 minutes make 120 minutes.

questions.prompt: A day has how many hours?
questions.rationale: There are 24 hours in one day.

questions.prompt: A film lasts 1 hour 35 minutes. How many minutes is that altogether?
questions.rationale: One hour is 60 minutes; 60 + 35 = 95 minutes.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks the basic hour-minute and day-hour facts with simple conversions; it does not address time zones or calendar-day exceptions.

lessons.explanation: An interval is the time from a start to an end. Find its length by comparing the two times, then order intervals from shortest to longest or longest to shortest as asked.

worked_example.prompt: A walk lasts 20 minutes and lunch lasts 45 minutes. Which lasts longer, and by how much?
steps: Compare 45 minutes with 20 minutes: 45 is greater.
45 − 20 = 25 minutes.

questions.prompt: Order these activities from shortest to longest: reading 18 minutes, drawing 12 minutes, walking 25 minutes.
questions.rationale: 12 minutes is shortest, then 18, then 25.

questions.prompt: A game takes 35 minutes. A puzzle takes 50 minutes. How much longer is the puzzle?
questions.rationale: 50 − 35 = 15 minutes.

questions.prompt: Three trips take 42, 28, and 36 minutes. Which order lists them from longest to shortest?
questions.rationale: 42 is greatest, followed by 36, then 28.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks comparing and ordering stated durations; it does not assess reading durations from a clock or timeline.

lessons.explanation: The minute hand points to the minutes; each number marks five minutes. The hour hand moves toward the next hour as time passes. Quarter past is :15 and quarter to is :45, in the hour before the named hour.

worked_example.prompt: Write twenty to four as digital time.
steps: Twenty minutes before 4:00 is 3:40.
The minute hand would point to 8; the hour hand is nearing 4.

questions.prompt: An analogue clock’s minute hand points to 5, and its hour hand is just past 7. What time is it?
questions.rationale: The 5 marks 25 minutes, and the hour hand is just past 7.

questions.prompt: How is quarter to 9 written digitally?
questions.rationale: Quarter to 9 is 15 minutes before 9:00: 8:45.

questions.prompt: Which clock-hand positions show 2:40?
choices: Minute hand on 8; hour hand between 2 and 3, nearer 3
Minute hand on 4; hour hand just past 2
Minute hand on 8; hour hand exactly on 2
Minute hand on 3; hour hand between 2 and 3
questions.rationale: The 8 marks 40 minutes; at 2:40 the hour hand is nearing 3.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw two clock faces: one showing 9:15 and one showing 3:40. Label each digital time.
checklist: Minute hands point to 3 and 8, respectively.
Hour hands are just past 9 and nearing 4, respectively.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks reading and interpreting five-minute clock times; the drawing task is not automatically assessed.

lessons.explanation: A unit square has area 1 square unit. Area counts unit squares covering a flat shape with no gaps or overlaps. Perimeter measures the distance around the shape’s edge, so area and perimeter describe different things.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangle has 4 columns and 3 rows of unit squares. What is its area?
steps: Count the squares: 4 × 3 = 12.
Each square has area 1 square unit.

questions.prompt: A shape is covered exactly by 9 unit squares with no gaps or overlaps. What is its area?
questions.rationale: Each unit square contributes 1 square unit of area.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 5 units long and 2 units wide. What is its area in square units?
questions.rationale: The rectangle has 5 × 2 = 10 unit squares.

questions.prompt: A 4-by-3-unit rectangle is covered with unit squares. Which statement is correct?
choices: Area is 14 square units; perimeter is 12 units.
Area is 12 square units; perimeter is 14 units.
Area and perimeter are both 12 units.
Area is 7 square units; perimeter is 14 units.
questions.rationale: Area is 4 × 3 = 12 square units; perimeter is 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 units.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check unit-square area and distinguish area from perimeter for simple rectangles. They do not assess irregular shapes or other area units.

lessons.explanation: Find a date in a calendar grid and read the weekday at the top of its column. For dates in one month, subtract the earlier day number from the later one. One week is 7 days: a full calendar row. A local calendar may mark holidays and season changes.

worked_example.prompt: How many days are between 6 June and 19 June?
steps: Both dates are in June.

questions.prompt: In this calendar, what weekday is 15 March?
questions.rationale: The 15 is in the Wednesday column.

questions.prompt: Use this March calendar. How many days pass from 4 March to 16 March?
questions.rationale: Subtract the earlier date: 16 − 4 = 12 days.

questions.prompt: Use this sample March calendar. How many whole weeks and extra days pass from 9 March to the holiday marked ★ on 30 March?
questions.rationale: From 9 to 30 March, 21 days pass: 3 full weeks with no extra days.

parent_activity.prompt: Use the current local calendar that marks a holiday or a family birthday. Ask the learner to locate and state today’s date in day-month form and its weekday, identify a marked event and its month, and count the days or weeks until it. Look for any season labels the calendar actually provides; if none are shown, say so rather than guessing.
checklist: Locates and states today’s actual date and weekday using the current local calendar.
Finds a genuinely marked holiday or birthday and correctly counts elapsed days or weeks until it.
Identifies a shown season label and month if present, or correctly explains that season information is not shown.

lessons.coverage_note: Digital questions check reading a supplied calendar grid and counting elapsed days. A parent observes use of a local calendar; season labels are checked only if actually shown.

lessons.explanation: When lengths join, add. When a piece is removed, subtract. Draw a bar showing the lengths, then write an equation with a box for the unknown length.

worked_example.prompt: A ribbon is 52 cm long. You cut off 19 cm. How many centimetres remain?
steps: Draw a bar labelled 52 cm. Mark 19 cm as removed and label the remaining part □. Write 52 - 19 = □.
Subtract in parts: 52 - 10 = 42, then 42 - 9 = 33.

questions.prompt: A string is 27 cm long. You attach another 16 cm of string without overlapping. How many centimetres long is it now?
questions.rationale: Joining the lengths means adding: 27 + 16 = 43.

questions.prompt: A rope is 45 cm long. You cut off 18 cm. How many centimetres remain?
questions.rationale: Subtract the removed length: 45 - 18 = 27.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is 68 cm long. You attach 17 cm without overlapping, then cut off 29 cm. How many centimetres remain?
questions.rationale: First add to get 85 cm. Then subtract 29 cm to get 56 cm.

parent_activity.prompt: A strip is 61 cm long, and 24 cm is cut off. Draw a labelled bar to show the story. Write an equation using a box for the unknown, then solve it.
checklist: The bar shows a total of 61 cm split into a removed 24 cm part and an unknown remaining part.
The equation uses a box for the remaining length and matches the story.
The solution is 37 cm and agrees with the labelled parts.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions partially check addition and subtraction with lengths within 100 cm. The activity separately checks drawing a representation and writing an equation with an unknown.

lessons.explanation: A day has two 12-hour halves. Times from 12 midnight until 12 noon are a.m. (morning). Times from 12 noon (midday) until 12 midnight are p.m. (afternoon and evening).

worked_example.prompt: Write 'twenty-five past four in the afternoon' as a digital time with a.m. or p.m.
steps: 'Twenty-five past four' means 25 minutes after 4 o'clock, written as 4:25.
Afternoon is after 12 noon (midday), so use p.m. to write 4:25 p.m.

questions.prompt: Morning school lessons begin at a quarter to nine. Which digital time shows when morning school starts?
questions.rationale: Quarter to nine is 8:45, and morning is before 12 noon, which uses a.m.

questions.prompt: An analogue clock has its minute hand pointing to 6 and its hour hand halfway between 7 and 8 during evening bedtime. What is the time?
questions.rationale: The minute hand on 6 means 30 minutes past 7, and evening is after midday so it is 7:30 p.m.

questions.prompt: Lunch starts 20 minutes after 12 noon, and quiet reading starts 15 minutes before 12 noon. Which shows both times accurately?
questions.rationale: Times just after 12 noon (midday) are p.m. (12:20 p.m.), while morning times before 12 noon are a.m. (11:45 a.m.).

parent_activity.prompt: Look at an analogue clock at three different times today (morning, afternoon, and evening) and write each time in digital format with a.m. or p.m.
checklist: Reads the hour and minute hands to the nearest 5 minutes
Labels morning times before 12 noon with a.m. and afternoon or evening times after 12 noon with p.m.
Explains why times just after 12 noon are p.m. and times just after midnight are a.m.

lessons.coverage_note: This multiple-choice quiz checks matching daily events and described clock positions to a.m. and p.m. times, but only partially covers reading real analogue clocks across the day.

lessons.explanation: Standard units measure length (m, cm, mm), mass (kg, g), and capacity (l, ml). When two measurements have the exact same unit, add or subtract their numbers directly.

worked_example.prompt: A jug holds 250 ml of water. You pour in another 400 ml of water. How many millilitres (ml) of water are in the jug now?
steps: Check that both amounts use the same unit: millilitres (ml).
Add the two amounts: 250 + 400 = 650 ml.

questions.prompt: A bag of flour has a mass of 350 g and a block of butter has a mass of 225 g. What is their combined mass in grams (g)?
questions.rationale: Both masses are in grams, so add 350 + 225 = 575 g.

questions.prompt: A wooden plank is 84 cm long. A carpenter saws off a 29 cm piece. How many centimetres (cm) of the plank remain?
questions.rationale: Subtract the piece removed from the starting length: 84 - 29 = 55 cm.

questions.prompt: A watering can holds 950 ml of water. You pour 320 ml onto tomato plants and 280 ml onto herbs. How many millilitres (ml) of water are left?
questions.rationale: Add the water used (320 + 280 = 600 ml) and subtract from the starting amount: 950 - 600 = 350 ml.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure a pencil in cm and mm with a ruler, weigh a food item in g or kg on kitchen scales, and measure two water amounts in ml with a measuring jug to add together.
checklist: Lines up the object at the 0 mark of the ruler to read centimetres and millimetres accurately
Reads mass on the kitchen scale in g or kg and reads liquid capacity on the measuring jug in ml or l
Adds two measurements that share the same unit accurately

lessons.coverage_note: This quiz checks adding and subtracting given measurements in the same unit, while physical measuring with rulers, scales, and jugs requires the hands-on parent activity.

lessons.explanation: To find how much longer or taller one object is than another, measure both objects in the same standard unit and subtract the shorter length from the longer length.

worked_example.prompt: Along a centimetre ruler starting at 0 cm, a paintbrush reaches 19 cm and a crayon reaches 12 cm. How much longer is the paintbrush than the crayon?
steps: Find both lengths in the same unit: 19 cm and 12 cm.
Subtract the shorter length from the longer length: 19 - 12 = 7 cm longer.

questions.prompt: A bookshelf is 145 cm tall and a desk is 78 cm tall. How many centimetres (cm) taller is the bookshelf than the desk?
questions.rationale: Subtract the height of the shorter desk from the taller bookshelf: 145 - 78 = 67 cm.

questions.prompt: A green ribbon measures 42 mm and a blue ribbon measures 29 mm. Which statement correctly describes their difference in length?
choices: The green ribbon is 13 cm longer
The green ribbon is 23 mm longer
The green ribbon is 71 mm longer
The green ribbon is 13 mm longer
questions.rationale: 42 mm minus 29 mm equals 13 mm, and the difference must keep the millimetre (mm) unit.

questions.prompt: Two sticks are placed next to a centimetre ruler as shown in the table. How many centimetres (cm) longer is Stick A than Stick B?
questions.rationale: Stick A is 34 - 0 = 34 cm long and Stick B is 26 - 5 = 21 cm long, so Stick A is 34 - 21 = 13 cm longer.

parent_activity.prompt: Choose two household objects (such as a book and a shoe), measure both with a centimetre ruler or tape measure, and state how much longer one is than the other.
checklist: Measures both objects accurately in the same standard unit (such as cm)
Subtracts the shorter measurement from the longer measurement to find the difference
States the comparison using the correct unit (for example, '8 cm longer')

lessons.coverage_note: This quiz checks calculating length differences from given measurements and ruler readings, while physically measuring real objects requires the parent activity.

lessons.explanation: A duration is the time between a start and finish. Count forward to the finish, or subtract the start time from the finish time. For times within one hour, crossing to the next hour may help.

worked_example.prompt: A show starts at 5:17 p.m. and ends at 5:43 p.m. How long is it?
steps: Count from 5:17 to 5:40: 23 minutes.
Count 3 more minutes to 5:43; 23 + 3 = 26.

questions.prompt: A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00. How long is it?
questions.rationale: From 10:15 to 11:00 is 45 minutes.

questions.prompt: A bus ride takes 35 minutes. A walk takes 40 minutes. How much longer is the walk?
questions.rationale: Subtract the shorter duration: 40 − 35 = 5.

questions.prompt: A film begins at 2:48 p.m. and ends at 3:26 p.m. How long does it last?
questions.rationale: 12 minutes reach 3:00, then 26 more make 38.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check durations within an hour, including crossing an hour; they do not cover overnight intervals.

lessons.explanation: Add prices by combining pounds and pence. To find change, subtract the total cost from the amount paid. Write money with two digits after the decimal point, so 75p is £0.75.

worked_example.prompt: A snack costs £1.35 and a drink costs 80p. You pay £5. Find the change.

questions.prompt: A book costs £2.40 and a pen costs 75p. What is their total cost in pounds?
You spend £3.68 and pay with £5. How much change do you get in pounds?
Two items cost £1.85 and £2.70. You pay £10. How much change do you get in pounds?

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check adding two prices and finding change from £5 or £10; they do not cover every money situation.

lessons.explanation: Choose a tool that fits the object: a ruler for small items, a metre stick for longer ones, or a tape for curved or flexible lengths. Start at zero. If the object begins elsewhere on the scale, subtract its start reading from its end reading.

worked_example.prompt: A strip starts at 3 cm and ends at 10 cm on a ruler. How long is it?
steps: Read the start: 3 cm; read the end: 10 cm.
Subtract: 10 − 3 = 7 cm.

questions.prompt: Which tool is most suitable for measuring the length of a pencil in centimetres?
questions.rationale: A ruler has centimetre marks suited to a pencil.

questions.prompt: An object begins at 4 cm and ends at 13 cm on a ruler. How long is it?
questions.rationale: Subtract the start reading: 13 − 4 = 9.

questions.prompt: A line is 1 m long. How many centimetres is that?
questions.rationale: One metre contains 100 centimetres.

parent_activity.prompt: Choose a small household object and measure its length with a ruler. Align zero with one end, then record the reading and unit.
checklist: The object is aligned with the zero mark.
The measurement is recorded with a suitable unit.

lessons.coverage_note: Questions check tool choice, an offset ruler reading, and metres-to-centimetres conversion. The activity provides a real measurement check.

lessons.explanation: Perimeter is the total distance around a flat shape. Measure each outside side, then add the lengths. A regular shape has equal sides, so multiply one side length by the number of sides.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangle has sides 6 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm, and 4 cm. Find its perimeter.
steps: Add the outside sides: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4.
The total is 20 cm.

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.rationale: Add the three side lengths: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.

questions.prompt: A square has sides of 7 cm each. What is its perimeter?
questions.rationale: A square has four equal sides: 4 × 7 = 28.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 9 m long and 2 m wide. How much fencing goes all the way around it?
questions.rationale: Add both pairs of sides: 9 + 2 + 9 + 2 = 22.

parent_activity.prompt: With an adult, measure each side of a small rectangular object, such as a book, using a ruler. Record each measurement in centimeters and add them to find its perimeter.
checklist: Line up the ruler’s zero mark with each side’s start.
Record each side length in centimeters.
Add all four measurements and compare the sum with the object’s perimeter.

lessons.coverage_note: The quiz checks perimeter calculations from given lengths. It does not assess physical measuring accuracy; the activity provides a practical check of ruler use and measuring.

lessons.explanation: Measure each object to the nearest whole unit and record its length. A line plot shows the counts: put a mark above each length, stacking marks when lengths repeat. Read the scale and count the marks to compare the data.

worked_example.prompt: Three measured lengths are 2 cm, 3 cm, and 3 cm. How many objects measured 3 cm?
steps: Write one mark above 2 cm and two marks above 3 cm.
Count the marks above 3 cm: there are 2.

questions.prompt: Lengths are 1, 2, 2, and 3 cm. How many objects measured 2 cm?
questions.rationale: The value 2 appears twice in the data.

questions.prompt: A line plot shows lengths: 1 cm has 1 mark, 2 cm has 3 marks, and 3 cm has 2 marks. How many objects were measured?
questions.rationale: Add all marks: 1 + 3 + 2 = 6.

questions.prompt: Lengths are 2, 2, 3, 4, and 4 cm. Which length occurs most often?
questions.rationale: Both 2 cm and 4 cm occur twice; 3 cm occurs once.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure four small objects to the nearest centimetre. Record their lengths and make a line plot with a mark for each object.
checklist: Each object has a recorded whole-centimetre measurement.
The plot scale includes every measured length.
Each measurement is represented by one mark.

lessons.coverage_note: The questions check reading counts and repeated values. The activity checks collecting measurements and constructing a plot; no drawn plot is assessed automatically.

lessons.explanation: A unit is the size of each step used to measure. Smaller units fit more times along the same object, so they give a larger number. An inch is larger than a centimetre; for the same length, the centimetre count is greater.

worked_example.prompt: The same desk measures about 120 cm and 47 inches. Which unit gives the larger number?
steps: A centimetre is smaller than an inch.
More centimetres fit along the desk, so 120 is greater than 47.
worked_example.answer: The centimetre measurement gives the larger number.

questions.prompt: The same ribbon is measured in centimetres and inches. Which measurement number is usually greater?
questions.rationale: A centimetre is smaller than an inch, so more fit along the ribbon.

questions.prompt: A board is 36 inches long. Which is a reasonable centimetre measurement for the same board?
questions.rationale: One inch is about 2.5 cm; 36 inches is about 90 cm.

questions.prompt: The same table measures 150 cm or 59 inches. What does this comparison show?
choices: The table changes length between units.
The inch is smaller than the centimetre.
The centimetre is smaller than the inch.
A centimetre and inch are equal-sized units.
questions.rationale: The larger centimetre count reflects a smaller unit, not a longer table.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure one straight object with a centimetre ruler and an inch ruler. Record both readings and compare the numbers.
checklist: The same object is measured with both units.
Both readings include their units.
The student identifies which measurement number is larger.

lessons.coverage_note: Questions check how unit size affects the number and use an approximate conversion example; the activity checks measuring with two units.

lessons.explanation: A dollar bill equals 100¢. Quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies equal 25¢, 10¢, 5¢, and 1¢. Add their values. For change, subtract the cost from the payment.

worked_example.prompt: Find the value of one $1 bill, two quarters, one dime, one nickel, and three pennies.
steps: Add the bill: 100¢ + 68¢ = 168¢.

questions.prompt: You have two quarters, three dimes, one nickel, and four pennies. What is their total value in ¢?
A snack costs 65 cents. Which statement correctly shows its price in cents and dollars?
questions.rationale: There are 100 cents in one dollar, so 65 cents is $0.65.

questions.prompt: You pay for a $3.47 notebook with two $1 bills and eight quarters. How much change should you receive, in ¢?
questions.rationale: The bills and quarters total 400¢. Subtract 347¢ to get 53¢ change.

lessons.coverage_note: These are partial checks of counting stated US currency values, interpreting $ and ¢, and finding change; they do not check recognizing physical coins or bills.

lessons.explanation: Quarter past means 15 minutes after the hour: the minute hand points to 3. Quarter to means 15 minutes before the next hour: it points to 9.

worked_example.prompt: The minute hand points to 9. The hour hand is between 6 and 7, close to 7. What time is it?
steps: The minute hand at 9 means 45 minutes past the hour, leaving 15 minutes until the next hour.
The next hour is 7, so say 'quarter to seven'.

questions.prompt: An analog clock's minute hand points to 3. Its hour hand is just past 3. What time does it show?
questions.rationale: The minute hand at 3 means 15 minutes past. The hour hand shows the hour is three.

questions.prompt: A minute hand takes 60 minutes to turn all the way around. Starting at 12, it makes a quarter turn clockwise to 3. How many minutes pass?
questions.rationale: A quarter is one of four equal parts. Divide 60 minutes by 4.

questions.prompt: You want to show quarter to seven, not quarter past seven. Which hand positions are correct?
choices: Minute hand at 3; hour hand just past 7
Minute hand at 9; hour hand approaching 6
Minute hand at 7; hour hand approaching 9
Minute hand at 9; hour hand approaching 7
questions.rationale: Quarter to seven is 6:45. The minute hand points to 9, and the hour hand has nearly reached 7.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw two clock faces numbered 1–12, or use a movable-hand clock. Show quarter past three and quarter to seven. Trace the minute hand's clockwise quarter turn from 12 for quarter past.
checklist: Quarter past three has the minute hand at 3 and the hour hand just past 3.
Quarter to seven has the minute hand at 9 and the hour hand between 6 and 7, close to 7.
Traces clockwise from 12 to 3 and identifies this as one quarter turn taking 15 minutes.

lessons.coverage_note: These quizzes partially check reading hand positions and linking quarter turns to minutes. Drawing or setting hands and explaining the turn need observation during the activity.

lessons.explanation: On a Roman-numeral clock, I–XII mark the same hour positions as 1–12; IIII may stand for IV. IX marks the 9 o’clock position, so a minute hand there means 45 minutes. For 24-hour time, add 12 to p.m. hours from 1 to 11; midnight becomes 00 and noon stays 12.

worked_example.prompt: A Roman-numeral clock’s hour hand is between IV and V; its minute hand points to IX. What time is it?
steps: IX is the 9 position, so the minutes are 45.
The hour hand is nearing V, so the time is 4:45.

questions.prompt: A clock shows IIII for 4. What hour position does IX mark?
questions.rationale: IX is the Roman numeral for 9.

questions.prompt: Write 3:20 p.m. in 24-hour time.
questions.rationale: For 3 p.m., add 12 to 3: 15:20.

questions.prompt: Write 12:20 a.m. in 24-hour time.
questions.rationale: The hour after midnight is written 00; the minutes stay 20.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks Roman clock positions and key 12-to-24-hour conversions; it does not assess every clock-reading situation.

lessons.explanation: A smaller uniform unit covers less length, mass, or capacity each time, so you need more units to measure the same amount. The smaller count steps make it easier to describe a measurement precisely than using large units or an imprecise fraction of a hand span.

worked_example.prompt: A book is about 2 pencils long. About how many paperclips might measure the same length if each paperclip is shorter than a pencil?
steps: Each paperclip covers less length than a pencil.
The same book therefore takes more paperclips to measure.
worked_example.answer: More than 2 paperclips; for example, about 9.

questions.prompt: A table measures 3 hand spans and a bit. Which method can give a more precise length?
choices: Count identical small cubes along it
Guess the fraction of a hand span
questions.rationale: Identical small units give a consistent count and avoid estimating a leftover fraction.

questions.prompt: A small glass holds less than a cup. Which informal unit is more suitable for measuring its capacity closely?
questions.rationale: A teaspoon is a smaller unit, so it gives a more detailed count for a small amount.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is 4 large blocks long. Each small cube is one quarter of a large block. How many small cubes cover the ribbon?
questions.rationale: Each large block equals 4 small cubes, so 4 blocks equal 16 cubes.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure the same book first with pencils, then with identical paperclips. Record both counts and compare the results.
checklist: Uses the same book for both measurements
Lines up uniform units without gaps or overlaps
Records more paperclips than pencils if each paperclip is shorter

lessons.coverage_note: Checks how unit size affects precision and count across measurement contexts; it does not test formal metric conversions.

lessons.explanation: On an analogue clock, the minute hand shows minutes; each number marks 5 minutes. The hour hand moves between hour numbers. For durations, convert to the same unit before comparing. Estimates can be checked with a timer.

worked_example.prompt: Which is longer: 1 minute 20 seconds or 75 seconds?
steps: 1 minute = 60 seconds, so 1 minute 20 seconds = 60 + 20 = 80 seconds.
80 seconds is greater than 75 seconds.

questions.prompt: The minute hand points to 43 minutes, and the hour hand is between 7 and 8, closer to 8. What is the digital time?
questions.rationale: The hour is still 7; the minute hand shows 43 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which is a reasonable estimate for brushing your teeth?
questions.rationale: Brushing typically takes a few minutes, not seconds or hours.

questions.prompt: A walk lasts 2 minutes 10 seconds. How many seconds is that?
questions.rationale: 2 minutes is 120 seconds; add 10 to get 130.

parent_activity.prompt: Estimate how long an everyday activity will take, then time it and record the measured duration with its unit.
checklist: Writes an estimate before timing
Uses a timer to measure the activity
Records the measured duration in minutes or seconds

lessons.coverage_note: This partial check covers reading one clock time, estimating a familiar duration, and converting minutes to seconds; it does not assess all clock layouts or elapsed-time problems.

lessons.explanation: There are 60 seconds in 1 minute. Months have 28, 29, 30, or 31 days. February has 28 days in a common year and 29 in a leap year; a leap year has 366 days. These facts help you work out and check calendar durations.

worked_example.prompt: How many seconds are in 3 minutes?
steps: There are 60 seconds in each minute.
Multiply 3 by 60: 180.

questions.prompt: How many seconds are in 2 minutes?
questions.rationale: Each minute has 60 seconds, so 2 minutes have 120 seconds.

questions.prompt: How many days are in February in a leap year?
questions.rationale: February has 29 days in a leap year.

questions.prompt: A common year has 365 days. How many days are in 2 leap years?
questions.rationale: Each leap year has 366 days; 2 × 366 = 732.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks seconds per minute and leap-year calendar facts; it does not ask learners to list every month’s length.

lessons.explanation: For 1–11 p.m., add 12 to the hour to get 24-hour time; minutes stay unchanged. For hours 13–23, subtract 12 to find the p.m. hour. For 1–11 a.m., keep the hour; 12 a.m. becomes 00, and 12 p.m. stays 12.

worked_example.prompt: Convert 3:45 p.m. to 24-hour time.
steps: Add 12 to the hour: 3 + 12 = 15.
Keep the minutes, 45.

questions.prompt: Write 7:30 p.m. in 24-hour time.
questions.rationale: Add 12 to 7 to get 19; the minutes stay 30.

questions.prompt: What is 19:30 in 12-hour time?
questions.rationale: 19 − 12 = 7, and hour 19 is in the evening.

questions.prompt: A film starts at 18:25 and lasts 40 minutes. What time does it end in 24-hour time?
questions.rationale: Add 35 minutes to reach 19:00, then 5 more minutes gives 19:05.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks common 12-hour and 24-hour conversions and one short duration; it does not cover every midnight, noon, or elapsed-time case.

lessons.explanation: A rectangle’s area is the number of unit squares covering it. Split one side into two lengths, b and c. The full rectangle’s area is a × (b + c); the two smaller rectangles have areas a × b and a × c, so the total is a × b + a × c.

worked_example.prompt: Find the area of a 6-by-13 rectangle by splitting 13 into 10 + 3.
steps: Split it into rectangles: 6 × 10 = 60 and 6 × 3 = 18.
Add their areas: 60 + 18 = 78.

questions.prompt: A 3-by-(4 + 2) rectangle is split into 3-by-4 and 3-by-2 rectangles. What is its total area?
questions.rationale: The parts have areas 12 and 6; together they make 18.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 5 units wide and its length is 7 + 3 units. Which sum gives its area using the split?
questions.rationale: The two smaller areas are 5 × 7 and 5 × 3.

questions.prompt: Use a split to find 8 × 14 as 8 × (10 + 4). What is the area?
questions.rationale: 8 × 10 = 80 and 8 × 4 = 32; their sum is 112.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw a 5-by-9 rectangle on grid paper, split the 9-unit side into 6 and 3, and label the areas of the two parts and the whole.
checklist: Draws a rectangle with side lengths 5 and 9 units
Shows the split as 6 + 3 along the 9-unit side
Labels part areas 30 and 15 and whole area 45 square units

lessons.coverage_note: Checks rectangle decomposition and the distributive property through numeric examples; it does not cover other area formulas.

lessons.explanation: Tile a rectangle with unit squares and leave no gaps or overlaps. Count the squares in one row, then multiply by the number of rows. That product matches the tile count and is the area.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangle is 4 units tall and 6 units wide. How many unit squares tile it?
steps: There are 4 rows with 6 unit squares in each row.
4 times 6 is 24, so 24 unit squares cover it.

questions.prompt: A rectangle has 3 rows of unit squares and 5 squares in each row. How many unit squares cover it?
questions.rationale: Three equal rows of 5 make 15 squares, and 3 times 5 is 15.

questions.prompt: A rectangle has 4 equal rows of 6 unit squares. Why is the area 4 times 6?
choices: Add the side lengths to get the outside.
Multiply the longer side by itself.
Four rows of six count every tile once.
questions.rationale: Equal rows mean rows times one row counts every square once.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 8 units long and 7 units wide, fully tiled by unit squares. What is the area in square units?
questions.rationale: Eight rows of 7 squares give 56, and 8 times 7 is 56.

parent_activity.prompt: On squared paper, draw a 4-by-6 rectangle, outline each unit square inside it, count the squares, and write the multiplication that matches your count.
checklist: The rectangle is 4 squares by 6 squares.
Each inside unit square is outlined once, with no gaps or overlaps.
The count is 24 and the written multiplication is 4 times 6.

lessons.coverage_note: These items partly check rectangle tile counts and matching them to length times width. They do not score the drawing, other shapes, or measuring with a ruler.

lessons.explanation: Split a compound shape into rectangles that do not overlap. Multiply each rectangle’s length by its width, then add the areas. Count every part once.

worked_example.prompt: An L-shaped room consists of a 3 m × 5 m rectangle and a 2 m × 4 m rectangle joined without overlap. Find its area.
steps: Find each rectangle’s area: 3 × 5 = 15 m² and 2 × 4 = 8 m².
Add the areas: 15 + 8 = 23 m².

questions.prompt: An L-shaped floor consists of two rectangles joined without overlap: 4 m × 6 m and 3 m × 2 m. What is its total area in m²?
questions.rationale: The rectangles cover 24 m² and 6 m², giving 30 m² altogether.

questions.prompt: A T-shaped floor has an 8 m × 2 m top bar. A 3 m × 5 m stem extends below the bar without overlap. What is the total area in m²?
questions.rationale: Add the bar’s area, 16 m², to the stem’s area, 15 m².

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 10 m wide and 8 m tall. Remove a rectangle 4 m wide and 3 m tall from its upper-right corner. Split the remaining L-shape into rectangles. What is its area in m²?
questions.rationale: Split vertically: the left rectangle is 6 × 8 and the lower-right rectangle is 4 × 5. Add 48 and 20.

parent_activity.prompt: On squared paper, draw an 8 cm × 6 cm rectangle. Cross out a 3 cm × 2 cm rectangle at its upper-right corner. Divide the remaining shape into two rectangles and calculate its area.
checklist: The crossed-out corner has the stated dimensions.
The two rectangles cover the remaining shape without gaps or overlap.
Each rectangle’s dimensions and area are recorded; their areas sum to 42 cm².

lessons.coverage_note: These quizzes partially check area addition and missing side lengths. The paper task checks whether the learner can draw and decompose a shape independently.

lessons.explanation: A rectangle’s area is the number of square units covering it. Multiply its length by its width; write square units, such as cm², because area measures a surface.

worked_example.prompt: Find the area of a rectangle 7 cm long and 9 cm wide.
steps: Use area = length × width.
7 × 9 = 63, so the area is 63 cm².

questions.prompt: A garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. What is its area?
questions.rationale: Multiply the side lengths: 8 × 5 = 40 m².

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 6 cm by 4 cm. What is its area?
questions.rationale: Area is length times width: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

questions.prompt: A rectangular floor is 12 m by 7 m. How many square metres of tile cover it?
questions.rationale: The floor has 12 × 7 = 84 square metres.

parent_activity.prompt: Draw two rectangles on square-grid paper, each with area 36 square units but different side-length pairs, not just rotated copies. Label the side lengths and explain how multiplying them counts the unit squares.
checklist: Both rectangles have side-length products equal to 36; for example, 4 by 9 and 6 by 6.
The drawn grid dimensions match the labels and the learner explains the rows-times-columns count.

lessons.coverage_note: The digital questions check multiplying whole-number side lengths to find rectangular area. Drawing, labeling, and representing products as rectangular areas are checked through the parent-observed activity and checklist, not the multiple-choice questions.

lessons.explanation: To convert to smaller units, multiply by how many fit in one larger unit. One kilometre is 1,000 metres, one hour is 60 minutes, and one week is 7 days.

worked_example.prompt: Convert 3 km to metres.

questions.prompt: How many metres are in 3 km?
questions.rationale: Each kilometre is 1,000 metres: 3 × 1,000 = 3,000.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are in 2 hours?
questions.rationale: Each hour has 60 minutes: 2 × 60 = 120.

questions.prompt: A trip lasts 5 weeks. How many days is that?
questions.rationale: Each week has 7 days: 5 × 7 = 35.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check three common conversions, not every measurement unit or conversions involving decimals.

lessons.explanation: Elapsed time is the time from a start to an end. Count forward in convenient steps, crossing an hour boundary when needed, or add the minutes and regroup each 60 minutes as one hour.

worked_example.prompt: A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes. When does it end?
steps: Add 45 minutes to reach 3:00.
Add the remaining 2 minutes: the film ends at 3:02.

questions.prompt: How many minutes pass from 9:20 to 10:05?
questions.rationale: From 9:20 to 10:00 is 40 minutes, then 5 more makes 45.

questions.prompt: A class starts at 1:35 and lasts 30 minutes. What time does it finish?
questions.rationale: Add 25 minutes to reach 2:00, then 5 more minutes.

questions.prompt: A train leaves at 10:48 and arrives at 12:17. How long is the trip?
questions.rationale: From 10:48 to 11:48 is an hour; then 29 minutes to 12:17.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks elapsed time in minutes across hour boundaries; drawing a number line is not assessed.

lessons.explanation: To compare measures, convert them to the same unit. For money, add pounds and pence carefully; 100 pence make £1. Estimation helps you judge whether a measure or total is sensible.

steps: Add £0.85 to get £4.70.

questions.prompt: Which is heavier: 1.5 kg or 1,200 g?
questions.rationale: 1.5 kg is 1,500 g, which is more than 1,200 g.

questions.prompt: What is the total cost of items priced £2.45, £1.30, and £0.75?
questions.rationale: Adding the three prices gives £4.50.

questions.prompt: Which is the most sensible estimate for the length of a classroom?
questions.rationale: A classroom is several metres long; the other choices are far too short or long.

lessons.coverage_note: This introductory quiz checks comparing mass, adding prices, and choosing a sensible length estimate; it does not assess estimating costs or measuring real lengths.

lessons.explanation: A quarter inch is ¼ inch, and two quarters make ½ inch. Measure to the nearest quarter-inch mark. On a line plot, each X represents one measurement, so count the Xs to find how many objects have each length.

worked_example.prompt: A ruler measurement is halfway between 2 and 3 inches. Write it to the nearest quarter inch.
steps: Halfway between 2 and 3 is 2½ inches.
Two quarters make a half, so this is 2¼ + ¼ = 2½ inches.

questions.prompt: A length is 3¼ inches. How many quarter-inch units is that?
questions.rationale: 3 inches contain 12 quarters; adding 1 quarter gives 13.

questions.prompt: Five pencils measure 4, 4¼, 4¼, 4½, and 5 inches. How many measure 4¼ inches?
questions.rationale: The length 4¼ inches appears twice in the list.

questions.prompt: A strip is 6½ inches long. How many quarter-inch lengths fit along it?
questions.rationale: Each inch contains 4 quarters, so 6½ × 4 = 26.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure five small objects to the nearest quarter inch and make a line plot using X marks above each length.
checklist: Each object is measured and recorded to a quarter-inch mark.
The plot labels its length scale and places one X for each object.

lessons.coverage_note: Checks quarter-inch units and reading a short data list; it does not assess a learner-made line plot.

lessons.explanation: Mass is measured in grams or kilograms; liquid volume is measured in litres. To find the total for equal groups, multiply the amount in one group by the number of groups.

worked_example.prompt: Three bags each weigh 250 g. What is their total mass?
steps: Multiply 250 g by 3: 250 × 3.

questions.prompt: Three bags each weigh 250 g. What is their total mass, in grams?
questions.rationale: Three groups of 250 g make 250 × 3 = 750 g.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 2 L of water. You pour out 1 L. How many litres remain?
questions.rationale: Subtract the litre poured out: 2 − 1 = 1 L remains.

questions.prompt: Four parcels each have a mass of 1 kg. What is their total mass in grams?
questions.rationale: Four kilograms equal 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 grams.

parent_activity.prompt: Choose an empty, open, watertight container. Estimate its capacity, then fill it using a marked measuring jug. Add the litres measured to find the capacity.
checklist: Record the estimate and measured capacity in litres.
Read the jug scale at eye level and record each amount added.

lessons.coverage_note: This quiz checks simple mass and volume calculations; estimating capacity and reading scales need hands-on practice.

lessons.explanation: Perimeter is the distance around a polygon: add its side lengths. Subtract known sides from the perimeter to find a missing side. Equal perimeters can enclose different areas.

worked_example.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle measuring 6 cm by 3 cm.
steps: Opposite sides match, so the four sides measure 6, 3, 6, and 3 cm.
Add the lengths: 6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18 cm.

questions.prompt: A rectangle has sides 8 cm and 5 cm. What is its perimeter in cm?
questions.rationale: Each length appears twice: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26.

questions.prompt: A pentagon has perimeter 30 cm. Four sides measure 4, 5, 6, and 7 cm. How long is the fifth side in cm?
questions.rationale: The known sides total 22 cm. The missing side is 30 − 22 = 8 cm.

questions.prompt: Two rectangles each have perimeter 24 cm. One is 8 cm long; the other is 7 cm long. How much greater is the second rectangle's area, in square cm?
questions.rationale: Length plus width is 12 cm. The areas are 8 × 4 = 32 and 7 × 5 = 35; their difference is 3.

parent_activity.prompt: Using a ruler and paper, draw two different rectangles with perimeter 24 cm and different areas. Label their side lengths, calculate each perimeter and area, and compare.
checklist: Both drawings have four right angles and measured side lengths matching their labels.
Each rectangle's four side lengths total 24 cm.
Length times width gives two different areas, labeled in square cm.

lessons.coverage_note: These quizzes partially check perimeter calculation, missing sides, and equal-perimeter area comparisons. The drawing activity checks construction separately; equal-area rectangles with different perimeters are not covered.

lessons.explanation: To change to a smaller metric unit, multiply: 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, and 1 kg = 1,000 g. For mixed units, convert the larger unit first, then add. A conversion table records matching amounts in two units.

worked_example.prompt: Convert 2 kg 350 g to grams.

questions.prompt: How many metres are in 3.5 km?
questions.rationale: Multiply kilometres by 1,000: 3.5 × 1,000 = 3,500 m.

questions.prompt: A conversion table shows 4 cm. What number of millimetres belongs beside it?
questions.rationale: Each centimetre equals 10 millimetres, so 4 cm equals 40 mm.

questions.prompt: A runner travels 1 km 250 m, then 800 m. What is the total distance in metres?
questions.rationale: Convert the first distance to 1,250 m, then add 800 m.

lessons.coverage_note: These questions check selected metric conversions and combining units, not every unit relationship or conversion-table format.

lessons.explanation: A rectangle’s area is length × width, measured in square units such as m². Its perimeter is the distance around it: 2 × length + 2 × width. A square has equal sides. Grid squares can help estimate an irregular shape’s area by counting full and partial squares.

worked_example.prompt: A rectangular room has area 48 m² and length 8 m. Find its width.
steps: Area = length × width, so width = 48 ÷ 8.

questions.prompt: A square has sides of 7.5 cm. What is its area?
questions.rationale: Area is side × side: 7.5 × 7.5 = 56.25 cm².

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 9 m long and 4 m wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.rationale: Perimeter = 2 × 9 + 2 × 4 = 26 m.

questions.prompt: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and has area 84 m². How many metres of fencing are needed to go around it?
questions.rationale: Its width is 84 ÷ 12 = 7 m; perimeter is 2 × 12 + 2 × 7 = 38 m.

lessons.coverage_note: This short quiz checks rectangle and square area and perimeter calculations; it does not assess irregular-grid area estimation.

lessons.explanation: To compare differently sized packs, find the price for the same amount, such as 1 kg or 100 g. Divide each price by its quantity in matching units. The lower unit price is better value if you can use the product; a larger pack can still be wasteful.

worked_example.prompt: Compare 2 kg of rice for $5.80 with 500 g for $1.60. Which costs less per kilogram?
steps: 2 kg costs $5.80 ÷ 2 = $2.90 per kg.
worked_example.answer: The 2 kg bag costs less per kilogram.

questions.prompt: Pack A has 2 kg of rice for $5.80. What is its price per kilogram?
questions.rationale: Divide the total price by the mass: $5.80 ÷ 2 = $2.90 per kg.

questions.prompt: Which is cheaper per 100 g: cereal A, 500 g for $3, or cereal B, 800 g for $4.40?
Juice A is 1.5 L for $3.60. Juice B is 2 L for $4.40. If you will use all of either pack, which is the better buy per litre?
choices: They cost the same per litre

lessons.coverage_note: Checks unit-price calculations and pack comparisons; it does not assess storage, waste, or personal preferences.

lessons.explanation: A unit cube has a volume of one cubic unit, such as 1 cm³. Count every cube, including hidden cubes. For a full cuboid, multiply the cube counts along its length, width, and height. Volume measures the space filled.

worked_example.prompt: A cuboid is 3 cubes long, 2 cubes wide, and 2 cubes high. Find its volume in 1 cm³ cubes.
steps: Each layer has 3 × 2 = 6 cubes.
Two layers have 6 × 2 = 12 cubes.

questions.prompt: A full cuboid is 4 cubes long, 2 cubes wide, and 3 cubes high. What is its volume in cubic units?
questions.rationale: Multiply the cube counts in each direction: 4 × 2 × 3 = 24.

questions.prompt: A solid has 5 cubes in its bottom layer and 5 cubes directly above them. How many unit cubes are in the solid?
questions.rationale: Count both layers: 5 + 5 = 10 cubes.

questions.prompt: A box is filled completely with 1 cm³ cubes. It is 5 cubes long, 3 cubes wide, and 2 cubes high. What is its volume in cm³?
questions.rationale: There are 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cubes, each with volume 1 cm³.

parent_activity.prompt: Estimate how many identical 1 cm³ cubes will fill a small empty box. Pack it completely, count the cubes, and compare the count with your estimate.
checklist: States an estimate before filling the box
Fills the box without gaps and counts the cubes
Records the measured volume in cubic units

lessons.coverage_note: The questions check counting cubes and finding cuboid volume; estimating by filling a box is checked only through the activity.

lessons.explanation: A number line places measurements in order and can show fractions or decimals. In word problems, use the units to choose an operation: divide for equal shares, add for totals, and subtract to find what remains. For elapsed time, add minutes and regroup every 60 minutes as 1 hour.

worked_example.prompt: Three ribbons measure 0.75 m, 1.2 m, and 0.95 m. Find their total length.

questions.prompt: A 2.5 kg bag of flour is shared equally among 4 people. How much flour does each receive?
questions.rationale: Divide the total equally: 2.5 ÷ 4 = 0.625 kg each.

questions.prompt: A journey takes 1 hour 45 minutes and starts at 09:20. What time does it end?
questions.rationale: 09:20 + 1 hour = 10:20; 45 more minutes gives 11:05.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 2.4 L of juice. You pour 0.75 L into one bottle and 0.85 L into another. How much remains?
questions.rationale: The pours total 1.60 L, and 2.4 − 1.6 = 0.8 L.

lessons.coverage_note: This short quiz checks sharing, totals, elapsed time, and subtraction with measurements; it does not assess drawing number lines.

lessons.explanation: A line plot places one mark above the number line for each measurement; repeated values stack. Read the marks to find counts, totals, or the difference between the greatest and least values. Rename fractions to a common denominator before adding or subtracting.

worked_example.prompt: Measurements are 1/4 inch, 1/2 inch, and 3/4 inch. Find their total length.
steps: Add to get 6/4 = 1 1/2 inches.

questions.prompt: Use the line plot. What is the total length of all four seedlings?
questions.rationale: Two quarter-inch lengths, one half-inch, and one three-quarter-inch length total 7/4 = 1 3/4 inches.

visual.title: Seedling lengths
visual.alt: Four marks: two at one quarter inch, one at one half inch, and one at three quarters inch.

questions.prompt: Use the line plot. What is the difference between the longest and shortest specimen?

visual.title: Specimen lengths
visual.alt: One specimen at each of one eighth, three eighths, five eighths, and seven eighths inch.

questions.prompt: Use the line plot. What is the combined length of all six objects?
questions.rationale: Three quarters, two halves, and one three-quarter length total 3/4 + 1 + 3/4 = 2 1/2 inches.

visual.title: Object measurements
visual.alt: Six marks: three stacked at one quarter inch, two stacked at one half inch, and one at three quarters inch.

parent_activity.prompt: Measure several small objects to the nearest eighth inch and make a line plot with one mark per object. Use it to find the shortest-to-longest difference and the total length.
checklist: Labels the number line in eighth-inch increments
Places one mark for each measured object
Uses plotted values to calculate a difference and a total

lessons.coverage_note: Questions check reading and calculating with provided fraction line plots; making a plot is addressed in the activity.

lessons.explanation: Metric and imperial units use different scales. Multiply or divide using approximate conversions: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds, and 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints.

worked_example.prompt: Using 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, about how many inches long is a 15 cm pencil?
steps: Each inch is about 2.5 cm, so divide 15 by 2.5.
Calculate 15 / 2.5 = 6.

questions.prompt: Using 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds, approximately how many pounds does a 35 kg child weigh?
questions.rationale: Multiply 35 kg by 2.2 pounds per kg to get 77 pounds.

questions.prompt: Using 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints, approximately how many pints are in a 4-litre jug?
questions.rationale: Multiply 4 litres by 1.75 pints per litre: 4 * 1.75 = 7.

questions.prompt: A shelf is 60 cm wide. Using 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, how many inches remain if you place an 18-inch box on the shelf?
questions.rationale: Convert 60 cm to inches (60 / 2.5 = 24), then subtract 18 to get 6.
